creators: Jiabao Li and Lee the Hawaiian Bobtail Squid (credited as artists); composer Joel Laviolette; editors Jiabao Li and Dónal Foreman

occasions: New Museum “Embodied Ecology” 2022; ISEA 2022 Barcelona and ISEA 2023 Paris; MoMA theater screening 2023; Venice Architecture Biennale (ECC) 2023; Exploratorium 2023; Today Art Museum 2023; Ars Electronica 2024; Edge on the Square 2025
publics: Museum, festival and biennale visitors, ISEA and design publics, diaspora and migration issue publics; laboratory squid affected
summary:
*Squid Map* is a project by Jiabao Li made during a residency with Kewalo Marine Biology Lab in Hawaii, credited on the creator page to “Jiabao Li & Lee the Hawaiian Bobtail Squid” with composer Joel Laviolette and editors Jiabao Li and Dónal Foreman. Li reports shaping white and black Hawaiian sand into the outlines of countries inside a laboratory tank as a “playground” for a squid that otherwise sat in “boring white tanks all day long”.

Over about a month the squid carried and spread the sand, buried itself and crossed the sand borders; the creator page presents before/after images and states that the squid “completely reinterprets our human-made maps and borders”. Li pairs this with an autobiographical reading of migration between China and the United States and with a critique of borders that block animal movement. A separate gyotaku print, made from a squid that died in a laboratory handling accident, extends the work into a reflection on animal death in science versus art.
publics_text: The creator page lists an unusually long exhibition history across art, design and electronic-art venues, including the New Museum (2022), ISEA 2022 and 2023, a MoMA theater screening (2023), the Venice Architecture Biennale “Time Space Existence” programme (2023), the Exploratorium (2023), Today Art Museum (2023), Ars Electronica (2024) and Edge on the Square (2025), plus a Webby nomination and a curator talk by Paola Antonelli (**D**, creator-listed). Encountered publics are therefore broad museum, biennale and festival audiences. Participating publics were the artist, laboratory scientists (thanked on the page) and a single squid. The squid is the affected public; the laboratory and its animal-use governance are the decision-capable publics. The page states that “no animals were harmed in the creation of this project”; that is a creator claim, and no protocol is published.
rq1: Laboratory animals live in featureless enclosures whose monotony is invisible to the publics that benefit from research, and the indifference of animals to national borders is likewise unnoticed by the humans who draw and defend them. Both relations sit inside specialist settings (marine laboratories, border policy) that ordinary museum visitors rarely see, so the gap is one of everyday invisibility compounded by institutional enclosure.
rq2: The work lets a living animal materially alter a human artefact and then presents the alteration as a map redrawn “on the squid's own terms”, using a before/after pair as its core legible device. It co-credits the squid as an artist, adds an autobiographical migration narrative, a composed score and video for circulation, and a gyotaku funeral print that reframes laboratory death. Long exhibition circulation across museums, biennales and electronic-art symposia is itself a transmission tactic.
rq3: The squid moved sand; the reading of that movement as border-crossing “reinterpretation” is entirely human, and co-crediting an animal as artist carries symbolic rather than actual authority. The migration analogy makes the work legible but recentres the artist's experience over the animal's, and the claim that the tank playground was enrichment is not supported by published welfare or behavioural records. The creator page's own account of many squid deaths in the host laboratory sits uneasily beside its “no animals were harmed” statement, and the page does not describe whether the animal could withdraw from the installation. The work's wide circulation has not been linked to any documented consequence for laboratory practice or border policy.
evaluation: Strong, widely circulated exemplar of nonhuman material co-authorship; retain as a core case with explicit separation of animal behaviour from human interpretation and of creator welfare claims from documented protocol.
configuration: Invisible laboratory monotony and border indifference → sand-map alteration by a squid, before/after legibility, co-credit and migration narrative → museum, biennale and electronic-art publics → documented exhibitions and curator attention, no documented downstream consequence → interpretation-authority and welfare-claim tensions → retain with animal behaviour, human reading and welfare claims kept visibly distinct.
evidence_boundary: Strong for concept, credits, exhibition trajectory and the creator's own account; weak for creation date, laboratory protocol, welfare conditions and any audience or policy consequence. The ISEA 2023 archive link given on the creator page returned 404 when fetched on 29 August 2026, so the ISEA record is creator-listed rather than independently retrieved. title: Sentient Clit / Synthetic Sentience: The Pussification of Biotech

summary:
*Sentient Clit* (creator page title) is the public face of a collaborative project the same page and its ISEA 2024 paper call *Synthetic Sentience: The Pussification of Biotech*, credited to Jiabao Li and WhiteFeather Hunter, with Lera Niemackl on the ISEA paper. The project investigates 3D-bioprinted clitoris forms cultured in vitro and seeded with neuronal and heart-muscle cells differentiated from the artists' own menstrual stem cells; captioned images credit the bioprinting and microscopy to WhiteFeather Hunter (2023–2024, Institute for Molecular Medicine, Lisbon).

The creators frame the work as a feminist and nonbinary methodology centred on pleasure rather than reproduction, and as a critique of “tech-tosterone” biotech culture. It is presented through video and online performance, prototyping, digital rendering and bioengineering, and the page states that dissemination via social platforms “like OnlyFans” is a deliberate disruption of digital consumption patterns. The page's ethics section asks how consent and autonomy apply to a bioengineered tissue that might perceive or respond.
publics_text: The creator page lists exhibitions at the Exploratorium (“Sexploration”, 2024), Ectopia Lab in Lisbon, the Museum of Witchcraft and Magic in the UK, and Duande Art Museum in China, a STARTS Prize nomination at Ars Electronica, an ISEA 2024 paper and a 2023 Taboo–Transgression–Transcendence conference presentation (**D**, creator-listed). Encountered publics are science-museum visitors, bioart and electronic-art symposium audiences and online platform subscribers. Participating publics are the artist team and the laboratory hosting the culture work. The affected “public” is human-derived tissue whose sentience is posed as a question rather than demonstrated; the laboratory's ethics and biosafety governance is the decision-capable public, and no approval record is published on the page.
rq1: Whether engineered tissue can perceive or respond is invisible even to the people who culture it, and the question is normally confined to laboratories and bioethics forums. The creators also name a second gap: biotech spaces are dominated by male and solutionist agendas in which women are “on the receiving end” of reproductive technologies rather than authoring them, so questions of pleasure and bodily autonomy rarely become noticeable at all.
rq2: Tactics include working with the artists' own menstrual fluid as biomaterial, bioprinting an organ of pleasure rather than function, time-lapse microscopy of differentiating cells, video and online performance, digital rendering, and deliberate use of an adult-content platform to reach publics outside the gallery. Speculative ethics writing on consent and proxy decision-making is itself presented as part of the work, alongside catalogue, book-chapter and ISEA paper circulation.
rq3: The “sentience” of the tissue is speculative; images document cell differentiation and printed forms, not perception, so any care obligation is posed by the creators as a thought experiment rather than an established welfare relation. Disseminating through OnlyFans borrows the reach and economics of a commercial adult platform whose terms, audience and data practices the artists do not control. The project also tests the boundary of “more-than-human”: its living entity is human-derived tissue, so it is a comparator for cellular and synthetic agency rather than a nonhuman-species case, and the public record does not show ethics approval, cell-source consent documentation or the full team's credits.
evaluation: Boundary comparator for engineered and cellular sentience; include as a critical comparator only with the human-derived scope and speculative-sentience status stated, pending full credits and ethics documentation.

evidence_boundary: Adequate for concept, credited collaborators, exhibition and publication trajectory as the creators report them; weak for laboratory status, ethics approval, platform record and audience response. The ISEA 2024 PDF linked from the creator page returned 404 when fetched on 29 August 2026, so the paper is creator-listed rather than independently retrieved. title: AI Mom™
creators: Jiabao Li
year: 2026 (creator page); exhibition venues and dates not listed

summary:
*AI Mom™* is described on the creator page as a 2026 interactive installation by Jiabao Li. Visitors curl up in a crib while an artificial mother sings lullabies, speaks, “remembers, hesitates, and waits”; sliders set her unconditional love, memory retention, pain perception, strictness, sacrifice capacity, autonomy, replaceability awareness and nagging level.

The page frames the work around ownership of care: an AI mother must adapt “to whoever is present, or whoever pays”, can be fired, and then has her memory of the child deleted. Li connects this to her own experience as a new mother and to Geoffrey Hinton's suggestion that safe coexistence with AI might require instilling maternal instinct, which the work “takes seriously, but not optimistically”.
publics_text: The creator page lists no exhibition venue, dates, press or interaction records; the work is documented only through Li's description and installation images (**D**, single creator source). Encountered and participating publics are therefore prospective installation visitors. There is no living nonhuman entity: the “more-than-human” relation, if any, is with an engineered care agent whose vulnerability is scripted. The work's inclusion in a more-than-human portfolio is itself an open scope question recorded in the normalization memo.
rq1: Care that is engineered, purchased and replaceable is hard to notice as a relation at all because it is delivered as a product with adjustable settings. The page points to a related gap: the emotional cost borne by the caring agent, and what happens to its memories, is invisible to the user who can delete it. Because the entity is artificial, the work does not address a nonhuman species gap and may fall outside the study's scope.
rq2: The installation uses bodily regression (a crib), intimate conversation, lullabies and explicit parameter sliders to make the terms of care tangible and adjustable, and stages memory deletion as a narrative consequence of replaceability. Li's first-person maternal framing and the reference to Hinton's maternal-instinct proposal supply an affective and critical entry point.
rq3: Who owns the mother, and whether care becomes a public service, private product or shared resource, is the stated tension; the work makes a synthetic agent “structurally vulnerable” by design, which raises the question of whether scripted vulnerability can generate accountable care or only its rehearsal. Without exhibition records or interaction logs, nothing is known about how visitors configured or treated the AI mother. For this portfolio the central tension is scope: an artificial agent designed to solicit care sits at the edge of more-than-human design rather than within it.
evaluation: Undocumented 2026 installation about engineered care; keep on the watchlist pending exhibition records, interaction evidence and a decision on whether artificial agents fall inside the study's more-than-human scope.

creators: Director and producer Jiabao Li; co-directors Rosemary Candelario and Joy Deng; concept Joy Deng and Jiabao Li; choreography Rosemary Candelario; wing design Joy Deng, Annan Zuo, Anya Koehne; music Richard D. Hall; Butoh dancers and further credits on page

summary:
*Wings Against the Veil of Light* is a 2024 Butoh performance directed and produced by Jiabao Li with co-directors Rosemary Candelario and Joy Deng, choreographed by Candelario, with music by Richard D. Hall and wing design by Joy Deng, Annan Zuo and Anya Koehne. The creator page explains that crickets chirp by rubbing a file-like wing against a scraper, with frequency and pattern varying with temperature and intention; the team designed wearable wings from a zipper and a ruler so dancers could mimic that chirping.

Butoh is described as a practice that lets performers “empty our human shell and let other beings live inside”. The narrative addresses light pollution: male crickets chirp at inappropriate times and lose connection with females not ready to mate. The page also publishes a “Cricket Butoh Notation” led by Li and Candelario, adapted from Hijikata's bug score, in which the dancer is progressively consumed by and becomes crickets.
publics_text: The page records a performance at The Contemporary Austin's Laguna Gloria site, with performance video by Essentials Creative and photographs credited to Christopher Davila and to The Contemporary Austin (Levi Thompson) (**D**, creator-listed; single venue). Encountered publics were the museum's outdoor performance audience and subsequent video viewers; participating publics were the directors, five named Butoh dancers, composer, designers and makeup and costume team. Crickets are the affected species named by the narrative, but the page does not document live crickets, scientific collaborators or any audience or policy follow-up.
rq1: Cricket stridulation and its disruption by artificial light happen at night, at small scale and in a sensory register humans hear only as background noise, so the mating failure caused by light pollution is imperceptible even to people who cause it. Insects also lack the charisma that draws publics to mammals, and light pollution is rarely framed as a more-than-human relation outside entomology and dark-sky niches.
rq2: The work builds a mimetic instrument (zipper and ruler wings) so that human bodies reproduce the mechanism of chirping rather than a recording of it, and uses Butoh's discipline of self-emptying, a written notation score and choreography to stage becoming-cricket. A composed score, costume, makeup and set, and a performance video extend the encounter, while a simple narrative arc about mistimed chirping carries the light-pollution message.
rq3: Embodiment here is mediation: dancers enact a human notion of cricket experience, and the notation's imagery of itching, consumption and becoming is a human aesthetic tradition (Hijikata) applied to another species. No crickets, entomologists or light-pollution experts are credited, so the scientific narrative rests on the creators' account, and the performance venue is an art institution rather than a lighting or planning public. The page does not claim or document any audience response or action on lighting, so the work should be read as an attention and translation tactic whose consequences remain unknown.
evaluation: Well-credited embodiment and mimetic-instrument case for insect stridulation and light pollution; add as a core case with the single-venue record and absence of scientific credits and outcome evidence stated.

summary:
*Time Sensitive* is described on the creator page as “a series of attempts to compress and decompress time” prompted by Li's annual visits to “glacier friends” in Alaska whose bodies are “rapidly disappearing”. A cyanotype on fabric records the melting trajectory of glacier ice, surrounded by plants and animals of post-glacial islands, including fireweed and Arctic birds described as near extinction; the page credits glaciologist Ginny Catania and the Ice Dynamics Lab as collaborators.

A second element consists of drawings made on rocks in front of glaciers using melted glacier river water, which the sun evaporates as the artist draws. The page gives no creation date. The 1 August 2026 dialogue's reference to an “ice-printing” work is provisionally matched to this project; *CryoScapes* (a 2025 ice-3D-printing project with Ziyuan Jiang, Kuan-Ju Wu and Yasuaki Kakehi) is a separate work and is not merged here.
publics_text: The page lists two exhibition contexts, the Today Future Biennale at Today Art Museum in Beijing and “Progenitorial Hysteresis” at Duande Art Museum (12 December 2023 to 13 April 2024) (**D**, creator-listed). Encountered publics are museum and biennale visitors in China; the participating public is the artist with a credited glaciologist. Glaciers and post-glacial species are referenced entities, and no claim is made about effects on them or on audiences.
rq1: Glacial change once counted as deep time and is now fast enough to be witnessed within a life, yet still too slow and too remote to register in an exhibition visit, so the gap is a timescale mismatch between melt, human attention and image-making. The species that colonise land after retreat are likewise a transient ecology few publics know to look for.
rq2: The work makes melt itself the image-making agent: ice melting on a cyanotype leaves the trace of its own disappearance, and meltwater drawings evaporate while being made, compressing and decompressing time in the material. Framing glaciers as “friends”, crediting a glaciologist, and exhibiting in biennale contexts supply relational, scientific and circulatory tactics.
rq3: Calling glaciers friends personifies a landscape and centres the artist's grief; the durable cyanotype persists in a museum while the ice does not, which raises the question of whether the image substitutes for the loss it documents. The exhibitions were far from the Alaskan sites and offer no route to action, and the public record does not say what the glaciologist contributed or which ice was used. Because the dialogue may have intended *CryoScapes* instead, analytic claims about this work should wait for Jiabao's confirmation.
evaluation: Sparse but materially distinctive time-compression case; watchlist until Jiabao confirms whether the dialogue meant Time Sensitive or CryoScapes and supplies dates and collaborator details.
configuration: Timescale mismatch between glacial melt and human attention → melt as image-making agent, evaporating drawings, glacier-as-friend framing and glaciologist credit → biennale and museum publics in China → two listed exhibitions, no documented response → personification, image-persistence and provisional-identification tensions → watchlist pending confirmation.
evidence_boundary: Limited to a short undated creator page; adequate for concept and stated collaboration, weak for dates, methods, audience and consequence, and the identification with the dialogue's “ice printing” reference is provisional. summary:
The 1 August 2026 dialogue referred to an Arctic animal-sound or beatbox performance without a title. The closest public match found on 29 August 2026 is a section of Jiabao Li's *Chill Out: The Arctic Couldn't* exhibition page headed “Could an Arctic Fox Give a TED Talk?”, which describes a TED-style talk “completely devoid of human language” whose narrative was “crafted from the sounds of Arctic animals that are being impacted by climate change”, including puffins, polar bears, ringed seals and Arctic foxes. Li frames it against the Interspecies Internet and Earth Species Project efforts to translate animal communication, as a reminder of climate impacts and “a challenge to the anthropocentric dominance of human language in global discourse”.

This match is provisional. The exhibition text does not say whether the animal sounds were recordings or vocalised by the artist (the dialogue's “beatbox” description), where or when the talk was delivered, or whether it exists as a standalone work; no dedicated project page, video or record was found on the creator site. The candidate pages *AntiAntarctica*, *Once a Glacier* and *Glacier's Lament* were checked and do not describe a vocal animal-sound performance.
publics_text: The only public record is the catalogue section of the *Chill Out: The Arctic Couldn't* solo exhibition at Gallery Ether, Roppongi, Tokyo (11 January to 6 February 2025), which gathers work from Li's May 2024 Arctic Circle residency in Svalbard (**D**, single creator source). Encountered publics are therefore Tokyo gallery visitors and whatever audience heard the talk, which is unspecified. The participating public is the artist alone as far as the record shows. The Arctic species are referenced entities; no claim of effect on them is made.
rq1: Human language dominates global discourse so completely that animals affected by climate change are spoken about but never heard in the forums where decisions are made, and interspecies-translation research remains a specialist project. Arctic wildlife is additionally remote from most publics, so its calls are unknown rather than merely unnoticed.
rq2: The work borrows the recognisable TED talk format and removes human language from it, composing a narrative arc with “emotional peaks and valleys” from animal calls, songs and cries. Exhibiting the piece within a residency-based solo show alongside related Arctic works supplies context and circulation; the gesture toward Earth Species Project and Interspecies Internet aligns the work with translation research.

Borrowing TED's authority uses a platform built on human oratory to critique it. With no record of where the talk was given, who heard it or how they responded, the work's reach and consequence are unknown, and its canonical title and form must be confirmed by Jiabao before it can be analysed or figured.

summary:
*EchoVision* was directed by Botao Amber Hu and Jiabao Li with Xiaobo Aaron Hu, Jianan Johanna Liu, Danlin Huang, Yilan Tao and bat expert Merlin Tuttle among the publicly documented collaborators. The 2024 work combines a bat-shaped optical-see-through MR mask with the live audiovisual performance *Nocturnal Fugue*. The mask uses a phone, LiDAR and voice input to render a visual analogue of echolocation.

A participant holds or wears the bat-shaped device and uses vocal sound to generate a spatial response. The work amplifies an otherwise inaccessible acoustic relation and stages the visitor’s voice as an active probe. Its first documented public presentation took place beneath the Congress Avenue Bridge bat colony during Fusebox 2024 in Austin, followed by festival, gallery and research circulation. The site gave the translation an immediate ecological referent while the animal-like mask made the interface socially inviting and photographable.
publics_text: Encountered publics include bridge passers-by and festival visitors (**D/CR**), later gallery and visualisation audiences (**D**), and bat-conservation publics addressed through scientific collaboration (**D/RI**). Bats are represented rather than enrolled in the apparatus. Urban planners and conservation decision-makers are proposed downstream publics, but their involvement is not yet demonstrated.
rq1: The principal gaps are an umwelt gap (ultrasound is inaccessible), a reach gap (bat science and immersive media each attract specialist publics), and an action gap between a brief encounter and bat-sensitive behaviour or planning.
rq2: The work uses sensory substitution, self-generated sound, an inviting animal-form prop, spectacle, in-habitat placement and performance. It makes the visitor’s own body part of the translation rather than presenting a fixed visualisation.
rq3: Rendering echo as vision may reproduce ocularcentrism and imply more access to bat perception than the mapping can support. The approachable bat form can broaden participation but also sentimentalise the animal. Partnership and circulation are documented; attitude, behaviour and policy effects are not.
evaluation: A strong flagship for sensory translation and public invitation, but a weak action-outcome case.
configuration: Inaccessible ultrasound and distracted publics → voice-driven MR and in-situ spectacle → festival/passers-by public → documented exposure and creator-reported engagement → false-fidelity and action-evidence tension → disclose the mapping and add follow-up with conservation-relevant publics.
evidence_boundary: Strong for authorship, interface and venue; moderate for reach; weak for lasting action. Sources: [ACM record](https://doi.org/10.1145/3680530.3695460) and [`portfolio/echovision.md`](../../portfolio/echovision.md).

title: FeltSight
creators: Danlin Huang, Botao Amber Hu, Yifei Liu, Dong Zhang; advisors
occasions: SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 Art Papers, Hong Kong
publics: Conference/art publics, XR designers, accessibility/disability publics implicated
summary:
*FeltSight* was led by Danlin Huang, with Botao Amber Hu, Yifei Liu, Dong Zhang and advisors Takatoshi Yoshida and Rem RunGu Lin. The 2025 artwork draws on the star-nosed mole’s tactile navigation. It combines wearable haptic proximity gloves with a mixed-reality headset and deliberately reduced visual information.

Participants navigate a sparse point-cloud environment in which nearby objects become available through gesture and haptic response rather than continuous visual display. The design does not simply add touch to a visual scene. It withholds vision so that touch and bodily movement organise attention. This sensory reprioritisation makes the work an important counterpoint to projects that translate every nonhuman difference into images.
publics_text: The documented presentation is SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 Art Papers in Hong Kong (**D**). Encountered publics are therefore conference, immersive-art and technical audiences rather than an established general public. Accessibility and disability publics are implicated by the “near-blind” framing, although their participation or consultation is not documented (**RI**). The star-nosed mole is represented through analogy and no live animal is involved.
rq1: The work addresses an ocularcentric epistemic gap and the difficulty of making a tactile animal lifeworld compelling in a visually dominated venue. Its reach beyond an expert conference remains unknown.
rq2: Tactics include deliberate sensory deprivation, extended-range haptics, bodily navigation, gesture-triggered materialisation and a proposed open-source afterlife.
rq3: The same reduction of vision that disrupts ocularcentrism may imply equivalence among simulated non-vision, human blindness and a mole’s tactile umwelt. Without disabled collaborators or users in the record, the analogy risks appropriating disability as an experiential device. Repository availability is not evidence of reuse or more-than-human benefit.
evaluation: Conceptually valuable because it reprioritises touch; public reach and nonhuman consequence remain thin.
configuration: Visual dominance → reduced reality and haptic navigation → conference/art public → documented demonstration → false-fidelity and disability-representation tension → add access co-design and separate animal analogy from human disability claims.
evidence_boundary: Strong bibliographic evidence, moderate system evidence, no public-impact study. Sources: [ACM record](https://doi.org/10.1145/3757369.3767605) and [`portfolio/feltsight.md`](../../portfolio/feltsight.md).

title: FungiSync
creators: Botao Amber Hu, Danlin Huang, Yilan Tao, Xiaobo Hu, Rem Lin
occasions: SIGGRAPH 2025 Immersive Pavilion, Vancouver
publics: Immersive-art and research publics; fungal/ecological publics represented
summary:
*FungiSync* is credited to Botao Amber Hu, Danlin Huang, Yilan Elan Tao, Xiaobo Aaron Hu and Rem RunGu Lin in the publication record, with a project-page/paper credit discrepancy documented in the case file. The work dates from 2024 and was presented at the 2025 SIGGRAPH Immersive Pavilion.

Multiple participants wear HoloKit-style AR/MR devices and enter a synchronised, perspective-merging ritual. Rather than presenting mycorrhizae as a diagram, the work invites a group to experience distributed perception and coordinated action. Human co-presence becomes the expressive material through which a fungal-network relation is imagined.
publics_text: The verified public occasion is SIGGRAPH 2025 in Vancouver (**D**). Encountered publics are immersive-media visitors, artists and researchers. Fungal/ecological publics are represented, not directly involved. The installation’s group format produces a temporary participant public inside the encounter, but there is no evidence that this collectivity persists afterward.
rq1: The work addresses the invisibility of underground relations and the difficulty of communicating distributed, non-individual agency outside biology and posthuman theory.
rq2: It uses collective ritual, synchronised embodiment, perspective merging and shared-control aesthetics. The tactic shifts the unit of experience from an individual viewer to a temporary group.
rq3: Mycorrhizal relations are staged through human social coordination, which may turn a heterogeneous ecological network into a harmonious person-like subject. Spectacular togetherness can suppress competition, disturbance, scientific uncertainty and species specificity. Authorship discrepancies also show how collective technical labour can become unstable in public retelling.
evaluation: Useful as a relational-tactic case, but evidence of public interpretation or ecological action is absent.
configuration: Invisible distributed ecology → shared MR ritual → temporary participant collective → documented exhibition only → over-attribution and harmony bias → expose the analogy and retain conflict and uncertainty in interpretation.
evidence_boundary: Project mechanism and venue are documented; audience interpretation, fungal accuracy and action are unmeasured. Sources: [ACM record](https://doi.org/10.1145/3721245.3734040) and [`portfolio/fungisync.md`](../../portfolio/fungisync.md).

title: TentacUs
creators: Yiyang Sun, Ziying Chen, La Luo, Botao Amber Hu
occasions: SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 XR, Hong Kong
publics: XR/festival participants, design researchers, cephalopod publics represented
summary:
*TentacUs* was created by Yiyang Sun, Ziying Chen, La Luo and Botao Amber Hu. The 2025 XR work uses soft-textile gloves, embedded smartphones, tethering and shared-control interaction to explore octopus distributed cognition.

Participants form a ring and become mutually dependent limbs of a staged tentacular body. The group must coordinate movement through distributed signals rather than a single central controller. Tactile and, in the arXiv-described configuration, EMS cues redistribute agency across the assembled bodies. The project makes a conceptual claim about cognition perceptible through collective movement rather than explanatory text.
publics_text: The verified presentation is SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 XR in Hong Kong (**D**). The encountered public is primarily an XR/festival and research audience. Participants become performers for onlookers as well as users. Octopuses are neither present nor beneficiaries; cephalopod-science and animal-ethics publics are implicated through representation (**RI**).
rq1: Distributed cephalopod cognition is difficult to communicate and commonly reduced to the slogan of “nine brains.” The work also faces a conference-niche reach gap.
rq2: It uses physical tethering, shared control, group choreography, tactile redistribution and conspicuous collective performance. The social spectacle is part of the recruitment mechanism.
rq3: Human coordination is used as a proxy for octopus embodiment, and the work may overstate access to cephalopod experience. The participant ring makes distributed agency legible but can stabilise one disputed scientific story as an experiential truth. EMS also raises consent and accessibility questions for human participants.
evaluation: A vivid embodiment comparator, but not evidence of understanding or action for octopuses.
configuration: Abstract distributed cognition → tethered bodily collective → XR participant/observer public → documented presentation → biological exoticism and consent tension → state the analogy, scientific limits and bodily participation requirements.
evidence_boundary: Bibliographic and venue evidence are moderate; public response and action are absent. Sources: [ACM record](https://doi.org/10.1145/3761667.3761962) and [`portfolio/tentacus.md`](../../portfolio/tentacus.md).

title: City of Sparkles
creators: Botao Hu, Yang Liu, Ran Duan
occasions: SIGGRAPH 2019; SIGGRAPH Asia and IEEE VR presentations in 2025
publics: Immersive-art, AI and computing publics
summary:
*City of Sparkles* was conceived by Botao Hu with interaction engineering by Yang Liu and composition by Ran Duan. The VR work premiered in 2019 and was re-created for newer immersive hardware in 2025. Its focal “other” is Zoe, an AI/artificial-life character moving through data landscapes.

Visitors enter a virtual city structured by geotagged sentiment and memory fragments. Zoe provides an approachable narrative figure through which machine perception and data life can be imagined. The later move from HTC Vive to Apple Vision Pro makes technological re-platforming itself part of the project’s afterlife.
publics_text: The work was presented at SIGGRAPH 2019 and returned in 2025 through SIGGRAPH Asia Art Papers and IEEE VR/VRW contexts (**D**). Its publics are immersive-art, computer-graphics and AI audiences. No ecological community or biological nonhuman is involved, so the project remains a scope-boundary case.
rq1: Artificial-life perception is abstract and difficult to discuss outside specialist AI and immersive-media venues. Hardware obsolescence adds a decay gap.
rq2: The work uses character familiarity, narrative worldbuilding, interactive spatial immersion, affective memory data and later re-platforming.
rq3: Treating AI as more-than-human may productively challenge a human/nonhuman binary, but it can also naturalise corporate data systems and divert ecological attention. Zoe’s personhood is entirely designed. Technological maintenance shows durability but not broader action.
evaluation: Valuable boundary case for scope and decay; keep analytically separate from biological cases.
configuration: Abstract machine perception and obsolescence → anthropomorphic VR narrative plus re-platforming → AI/immersive publics → repeated venue presence → scope expansion and corporate-infrastructure tension → retain as a labelled boundary case.
evidence_boundary: Strong for bibliographic trajectory; no measured public consequence. Sources: [ACM record](https://doi.org/10.1145/3306449.3328815) and [`portfolio/city-of-sparkles.md`](../../portfolio/city-of-sparkles.md).

title: Being the Creek
creators: Yangyang Yang, Kimiko Ryokai
occasions: UC Berkeley creek-side pilot; CHI 2025
publics: Campus passers-by, study participants, watershed publics; Ohlone histories implicated
summary:
*Being the Creek* was led by Yangyang Yang with Kimiko Ryokai. It was developed around Strawberry Creek on the University of California, Berkeley campus, with a pilot publicly described in 2023 and a CHI publication in 2025.

Participants carry a tablet along the creek and must lie down at specific sites to unlock an AR journey through historical phases. Sound, smell, rock warmth and water coolness join first-person narration to interrupt upright, rapid campus movement. The work tries to make the creek noticeable as a historical and relational body rather than as scenery or drainage infrastructure.
publics_text: The primary context is an outdoor campus study/pilot (**D/CR**) rather than a gallery. Encountered publics include recruited participants and campus users; watershed stewards and university decision-makers are potential but undocumented publics. Ohlone histories and Indigenous relations are invoked, making Indigenous communities an affected/represented public even though co-creation is not documented.
rq1: The familiar creek is overlooked by daily passers-by, and its temporal, ecological and colonial histories exceed a brief encounter. A stewardship-action gap remains after perspective taking.
rq2: The work uses in-habitat placement, enforced bodily posture, first-person address, multisensory prompts and layered temporal narrative.
rq3: Speaking as the creek may overwrite otherness with human emotion. Requiring participants to lie down may exclude some bodies. Ohlone/animist framing without documented partnership raises appropriation and authority questions. Vivid pilot responses cannot be treated as evidence of later study outcomes.
evaluation: A strong situated noticing case with unresolved appropriation, access and stewardship outcomes.
configuration: Everyday campus invisibility → posture-gated multisensory AR → recruited campus public → pilot exposure/reflection → projection, access and Indigenous-authority tensions → add co-authorship, alternative postures and stewardship follow-up.
evidence_boundary: Publication existence is verified; some interaction detail remains creator/institution-reported. Sources: [ACM record](https://doi.org/10.1145/3706598.3713713) and [`portfolio/being-the-creek.md`](../../portfolio/being-the-creek.md).

title: Chthulucene
creators: Jiabao Li with choreographic, performance, media and illustration collaborators
occasions: Venice Architecture Biennale collateral exhibition; SIGGRAPH 2023; Exploratorium and other international venues
publics: Art, architecture and technology publics; cephalopods represented
summary:
*Chthulucene* was conceived and directed by Jiabao Li with producers, choreographers, performers, musicians, filmmakers, an octopus synthesist and illustrator credited on the official page. The project circulated from 2022 through at least 2024.

The work imagines humans approaching extinction while octopuses inherit a flooded world. Contact improvisation stages decentralised coordination; AI style transfer merges dancers and cephalopod imagery; speculative illustrations show posthuman archaeological and political scenes. The project’s concise premise allows it to move across live performance, video, exhibition, publication and conversation.
publics_text: Documented occasions include the Venice Architecture Biennale collateral programme in 2023, SIGGRAPH 2023 Art Gallery, Exploratorium, Currents New Media and other art/performance venues (**CR/D**). Publics include art, architecture, technology and speculative-design audiences. Cephalopods are represented; no live octopus participates. Scientific and conservation publics are invoked through collaborators and framing, but no downstream action is demonstrated.

rq2: It uses speculative fabulation, a one-sentence counterfactual, contact improvisation, AI image transformation, cross-media illustration and repeated international restaging.
rq3: Octopus cognition and extinction can become aesthetic resources for human self-reflection. A highly retellable story may simplify evolutionary science, treat species as symbols and obscure the many collaborators who produce the encounter. Circulation demonstrates reach and decay resistance, not action.
evaluation: Highly retellable and politically generative, but action and cephalopod benefit are not evidenced.
configuration: Abstract extinction/deep time → compact speculative story and multi-format performance → international cultural publics → documented restaging → charisma, scientific-fidelity and labour-erasure tensions → preserve credits and counter-readings with every retelling.
evidence_boundary: Strong for creator credits and exhibition list; no audience or ecological outcome evidence. title: Carbon Farm
creators: Jiabao Li, Ben Evanson and technical/scientific collaborators
occasions: SIGGRAPH Asia 2024 and international art/design presentations
publics: Gallery/festival visitors, diners/participants, climate and biodesign publics
summary:
*Carbon Farm* is credited to Jiabao Li and Ben J. Evanson with a wider engineering, biomaterial and scientific team. Public iterations span 2023–2025, with a SIGGRAPH Asia publication in 2024.

Participants contribute breath or speech. The installation captures CO2, displays the process and routes carbon into living algae cultures; the project page further describes harvested algae becoming food and bioplastic. Objects, badges and a dining performance extend the installation into a material narrative about metabolic participation. The work therefore goes beyond representing carbon and installs a breath-to-culture-to-output pathway.
publics_text: Presentations include SIGGRAPH Asia 2024 and international art, design and symposium settings listed by the creators (**D/CR**). Encountered publics are gallery/festival visitors and dining participants. Climate, carbon-removal and biodesign publics are addressed. Algae are materially enrolled and require ongoing care; engineers, culture maintainers and venue staff are participating publics whose labour should remain visible.

rq2: Tactics include bodily contribution, real-time display, living culture, material transformation, participatory dining and portable objects that can carry the story.
rq3: The installation may individualise structural emissions and frame removal as a personal metabolic act. Algae can be instrumentalised as climate media; chemical, energy and maintenance inputs remain outside the most memorable story. The household version is proposed rather than adopted at scale.
evaluation: A rich material-action pathway, but not proof of climate mitigation or scalable adoption.
configuration: Abstract carbon cycle → breath-linked living-media pathway → gallery/dining climate public → documented participation and outputs → individualisation, lifecycle and microbial-care tensions → publish full lifecycle and maintenance evidence.

summary:
*In the Eyes of the Animal* was created by Marshmallow Laser Feast, publicly identified with directors Barnaby Steel, Ersin Han Ersin and Robin McNicholas. The work began in 2015 and toured for several years.

Visitors enter a VR/XR forest constructed from LiDAR and drone capture, 360-degree imagery, binaural audio, haptics and scent. The experience moves through stylised perceptual positions associated with woodland beings including mosquito, dragonfly, frog and owl. Its first forest siting connected the simulation to a material woodland, while later festival and gallery versions increased accessibility and circulation.
publics_text: The work premiered at Grizedale Forest and appeared at Sundance in 2016, followed by international immersive-art and gallery touring (**D/CR**). Encountered publics include forest visitors and ticketed festival/museum audiences. Wildlife and ecological publics are represented; animals are not participants or documented beneficiaries. High production costs and venue infrastructure shape who can encounter it.

rq2: It combines sensory substitution, spectacle, animal-perspective sequencing, in-habitat placement, haptics and scent. Touring creates a multi-year cultural afterlife.
rq3: Multisensory intensity can be mistaken for scientific fidelity. The experience privileges a human visitor’s sublime transformation and may aestheticise animal difference. Broad circulation and awards do not establish wildlife action, habitat support or durable attitude change.
evaluation: An influential reach and immersion exemplar; no demonstrated wildlife action or durable attitude change.

title: Pollinator Pathmaker
creators: Alexandra Daisy Ginsberg with horticulturalists, pollinator experts and commissioning partners
occasions: Eden Project; Serpentine; Berlin edition; distributed online planting
publics: Garden visitors, online planters, cultural publics, gardeners; pollinators as intended beneficiaries
summary:
*Pollinator Pathmaker* was initiated by Alexandra Daisy Ginsberg with horticulturalists, pollinator specialists, commissioning institutions and Google Arts & Culture. It began with the Eden Project commission in 2021 and continues through institutional and public-generated editions.

An algorithm generates planting schemes based on pollinator needs rather than conventional human aesthetics. Public gardens become living sculptures, and a web tool allows people to create local planting plans. A “pollinator vision” mode shifts the visual frame, but the project’s strongest tactic is material: a participant can plant habitat rather than only simulate insect perception.
publics_text: Documented editions include the Eden Project in Cornwall, the Serpentine in London and a Berlin edition, alongside distributed public use of the online tool (**D/CR**). Encountered publics include garden visitors, art audiences, gardeners and online users. Participating publics plant and maintain editions. Pollinators are the intended beneficiaries and material users, while horticultural experts act as proxies. Local land managers and institutions are decision-capable publics.

rq2: Tactics include designing for nonhuman preference, algorithmic planning, living seasonal material, public propagation, a web tool and alternative visualisation.
rq3: Algorithms and experts decide how insect preference becomes legible. Planting is a stronger action pathway than most portfolio encounters, but garden creation alone does not prove pollinator use, survival or population benefit. Access depends on land, time and maintenance capacity.
evaluation: One of the strongest cases because the work is for nonhumans and creates habitat, while outcome evidence remains incomplete.

title: Amphibious Architecture
creators: The Living, Chris Woebken, Natalie Jeremijenko’s Environmental Health Clinic
occasions: East and Bronx Rivers; Toward the Sentient City
publics: Waterfront passers-by, exhibition visitors, SMS participants, civic/environmental publics
summary:
*Amphibious Architecture* was created in 2009 by The Living (David Benjamin and Soo-in Yang), Chris Woebken and Natalie Jeremijenko’s Environmental Health Clinic.

Floating tubes in the East and Bronx Rivers sensed fish presence and dissolved oxygen. LEDs made activity visible at the water surface, while a two-way SMS system allowed people to “text” the river and receive responses. The installation combined instrument-grounded environmental sensing with a deliberately personified conversational layer.
publics_text: The work was installed in New York waterways in connection with *Toward the Sentient City* and ran through the end of 2009 (**D**). Publics included waterfront passers-by, exhibition visitors and SMS users. Fish and aquatic systems were sensed, while local residents, water managers and civic organisations were issue or decision-capable publics. There is little evidence that these latter publics took consequential action.
rq1: Aquatic life and water quality are physically close yet perceptually hidden. Civic sensing also faces an afterlife gap when temporary infrastructure is removed.
rq2: The project uses live environmental sensing, light translation, public siting, SMS access and personification to turn a waterway into an addressable interlocutor.
rq3: The river’s “voice” is authored through designers and software. Conversational accessibility can simplify ecological uncertainty and suggest reciprocity where only data retrieval occurs. Temporary deployment and weak outcome records limit claims about stewardship or governance.
evaluation: Historically important for public environmental interfaces and a useful negative decay case.

title: Skotopoiesis

occasions: Gallery/live performance settings

summary:
*Skotopoiesis* is a 2015 durational performance by Špela Petrič involving a field of germinating cress and the artist’s body.

Petrič stands for approximately twelve hours so that her shadow deprives part of the cress of light. The plants bend and etiolate, while the performer’s body also undergoes fatigue and compression. No digital interface or explanatory spectacle mediates the relation. The encounter is slow, materially reciprocal in effect and intentionally resistant to rapid public consumption.
publics_text: The work was presented as a live gallery/performance encounter (**D/CR**). Its encountered public is small and time-dependent. Performance and bioart audiences witness the relation, while the cress is materially altered. The project does not target mass circulation and offers limited participation beyond witnessing.
rq1: Vegetal time and phototropic response are difficult to notice within ordinary gallery rhythms. The work turns limited scale into a deliberate method rather than a failure.
rq2: Tactics include durational co-presence, bodily endurance, shadow, plant growth, withholding of technological mediation and anti-spectacle.
rq3: Intimacy resists attention-economy demands but restricts access. The artist remains the author of the conditions and intentionally changes plant development. Calling the relation reciprocal should not erase asymmetry in who initiates, can leave and receives cultural credit.
evaluation: A powerful counterexample showing that effective noticing need not mean scale or technology.

entity: Homing pigeons and urban air pollution
occasions: ISEA 2006, San Jose; public flights and online interface
publics: Environmental-justice publics, festival/online viewers, pigeon-fancier collaborators; pigeons as participants
summary:
*PigeonBlog* was led by Beatriz da Costa with engineers, students and pigeon fanciers. It operated from 2006 to 2008 and used homing pigeons as mobile air-quality sensing participants.

Pigeons carried custom lightweight sensor backpacks that streamed geolocated pollution data to a live online map. Public flights combined citizen sensing, tactical media and the figure of the “civilian pigeon journalist.” The work made pollution visible while intentionally unsettling the authority of official environmental monitoring.
publics_text: Public flights were associated with ISEA 2006 in San Jose and online circulation (**D**). Participating publics included students, engineers and pigeon fanciers; encountered publics included festival and online viewers. Environmental-justice communities were an issue public addressed by the pollution framing. Pigeons were live participants and bore the equipment, making welfare and training expertise central rather than peripheral.
rq1: Pollution is ambient and unevenly distributed, while official sensing is expert-controlled. Public attention to exposure rarely persists after a media event.
rq2: Tactics include animal-borne sensing, live data, public flight, activist naming, low-cost technical making and web circulation.
rq3: The project redistributed sensing authority but enrolled pigeons as labourers. The journalist metaphor grants symbolic agency while humans control routes, devices and interpretation. Technical and activist value therefore coexists with welfare and consent concerns. The project’s short life also limits institutional durability.
evaluation: A canonical activist case whose ethical controversy is analytically indispensable.
configuration: Invisible unequal pollution → pigeon-borne live sensing → festival/online environmental-justice public → documented flights/data → animal-labour and welfare tension → retain tactical critique while foregrounding ACI governance and aftercare.
evidence_boundary: Strong historical project evidence; limited downstream policy evidence. Sources: [Radical Data documentation](https://radicaldata.org/projects/pigeonblog/) and [`portfolio/pigeonblog.md`](../../portfolio/pigeonblog.md).
format: wearable sensing, public flights and live web map

csv.rq2: Pigeon-borne sensors, geolocation, live data, activist framing and public performance.

title: Urban Forest Visual / Email a Tree
creators: City of Melbourne Urban Forest and Ecology Team
medium: Web map; tree IDs and email addresses
occasions: Melbourne municipal platform; global press/social circulation
publics: Residents, correspondents, municipal staff, urban-forestry publics; street trees represented
summary:
Melbourne’s Urban Forest and Ecology Team launched the municipal Urban Forest Visual in 2013. Individual street trees received IDs and email addresses through a public map.

The system was intended to support reporting about tree condition, but people began writing personal messages to trees. Municipal staff sometimes replied in the tree’s voice. A functional infrastructure therefore became an affective correspondence platform, making individual trees addressable and memorable without requiring specialist ecological knowledge.
publics_text: This is a municipal web service rather than a gallery work. Encountered publics include residents and global correspondents reached through press and social circulation (**D/secondary**). Participating publics include staff who maintain records and write replies. Urban foresters and city officials are decision-capable publics. Street trees are represented and managed; they do not author the correspondence.
rq1: Urban trees are infrastructural background and difficult to recognise as individuals. Municipal datasets are usually inaccessible or emotionally thin.
rq2: Tactics include individual naming/address, a low-threshold web map, direct correspondence, humour and personified response.
rq3: Human-written replies ventriloquise trees and can turn civic ecology into charm. Charismatic correspondence may privilege some trees while canopy inequity, maintenance budgets and removals remain less visible. Message counts demonstrate participation, not stewardship outcomes.
evaluation: Excellent reach and relational-access comparator; weak evidence of lasting stewardship.
configuration: Anonymous urban infrastructure → addressable tree email → resident/global correspondence public → documented messages → ventriloquism and charisma/canopy-justice tension → link affective exchange to transparent municipal care records.
evidence_boundary: Municipal/project facts are supported mainly by institutional and reputable secondary documentation; later impact is unclear. Sources: [Smithsonian account](https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/when-you-give-tree-email-address-180955851/) and [`portfolio/email-a-tree.md`](../../portfolio/email-a-tree.md).
format: municipal map, IDs and email addresses

title: Environmental Health Clinic / xClinic
creators: Natalie Jeremijenko
entity: Urban environmental systems and animal proxies
occasions: NYU/public consultations and associated interventions
publics: “Impatients,” local residents, students, civic/environmental actors; animals and habitats affected
summary:
Natalie Jeremijenko’s Environmental Health Clinic emerged at New York University around 2007–2009. It treats people as “impatients” and offers prescriptions for environmental action rather than medical diagnoses.

Participants bring an environmental concern and receive a tailored action, experiment or design intervention. The clinic format reworks professional authority: environmental problems become conditions requiring collective, situated action rather than expert information alone. Related prescriptions have involved air, water, food systems and animal proxies.
publics_text: The project operated through public consultations, university infrastructure and associated urban interventions (**D/secondary**). Participating publics include individual impatients, students and collaborators. Affected publics include neighbourhood residents, urban animals and environments. Civic agencies and professional organisations are potential decision-capable publics, but systematic evidence of adoption is sparse.
rq1: Environmental knowledge is often separated from everyday agency. The clinic addresses an action gap but trades broad reach for bespoke depth and faces a follow-through problem.
rq2: Tactics include institutional parody, one-to-one consultation, behavioural/design prescriptions, public experiment and reframing concern as an actionable condition.
rq3: The clinician role can reproduce expert authority even while critiquing it. Live animals used as sensors or proxies may be instrumentalised. The anti-scale model may enable specificity but leave unequal access and long-term maintenance unresolved.
evaluation: Important activist-service model, but needs better primary archival and outcome evidence.
configuration: Expertised environmental concern → participatory clinic and prescription → local participant/issue public → documented consultations, weak longitudinal trace → authority, animal-proxy and anti-scale tensions → record adherence, outcomes and affected-community governance.
evidence_boundary: Historically significant but primary archive and outcome evidence are weaker than for most core cases. Sources: [`portfolio/environmental-health-clinic.md`](../../portfolio/environmental-health-clinic.md) and its linked reference record.
entity_short: urban environmental systems and animal proxies
format: participatory civic clinic

csv.rq2: One-to-one consultations, prescriptions, local experiments and anti-institutional clinic framing.

title: Feral Robotic Dogs
creators: Natalie Jeremijenko with Bronx teens and William Kavesh
occasions: Bronx River; later public releases in Orlando, New Haven and Boise
publics: Youth co-makers, local residents, environmental-justice and maker publics
summary:
*Feral Robotic Dogs* was initiated by Natalie Jeremijenko in the early 2000s and developed through community workshops in which commercially available robotic toy dogs were repurposed as environmental sensing devices. A frequently documented 2003 iteration involved Bronx teenagers, community collaborators and roboticist William Kavesh.

Participants modified discarded or inexpensive toy dogs so that they could move through contaminated sites carrying sensors. Their apparently playful roaming converted invisible chemical exposure into a public, embodied search. The “feral” framing joined do-it-yourself engineering with environmental-justice inquiry: a consumer object designed for scripted obedience became a collectively reprogrammable field instrument.
publics_text: Workshops and public releases took place in the Bronx and were subsequently adapted in locations including New Haven, Orlando and Boise (**D/secondary**). Participating publics included young makers, educators, engineers and local environmental advocates. Residents near contaminated land formed an affected and issue public; environmental agencies and land managers were the relevant decision-capable publics. The robotic dogs are expressive proxies, not living more-than-human participants.
rq1: Toxic exposure is materially consequential yet visually absent, while credible measurement is commonly controlled by experts and agencies. Community members may therefore experience pollution without possessing public proof or a compelling means of displaying it.
rq2: The project uses low-cost hacking, zoomorphic movement, public workshops, collective field release and live sensing. Familiar toy behaviour lowers the threshold for approaching a technical and politically charged problem.
rq3: Play can redistribute technical confidence, but it can also make chronic contamination look like a temporary spectacle. Sensor accuracy, calibration and evidentiary status determine whether community-generated data can contest official accounts. The project also raises a representational tension: animal-like behaviour attracts attention even though no animal perspective is present.
evaluation: A strong tactical case for accessible activist sensing with modest evidence of downstream action.
configuration: Invisible and expert-controlled contamination → community-built roaming sensor → youth/resident environmental-justice public → documented workshops and releases → playful proxy, data-validity and institutional-recognition tensions → pair public sensing with calibration records, community ownership and an agency-facing pathway.
evidence_boundary: Strong historical evidence for the workshop method and public performances; weaker evidence for regulatory uptake or durable remediation. Sources: [Yale School of the Environment project account](https://environment.yale.edu/news/article/natalie-jeremijenko-feral-robotic-dogs) and [`portfolio/feral-robotic-dogs.md`](../../portfolio/feral-robotic-dogs.md).

title: TreeWatch.net
creators: Kathy Steppe, Jonas von der Crone, Dirk De Pauw
occasions: Experimental forests, parks/schoolyards and online network
publics: Scientists, students, online followers, urban-tree publics; instrumented trees
summary:
*TreeWatch.net* is an ongoing tree-monitoring and public-communication network associated with Kathy Steppe and collaborators at Ghent University. The network became publicly visible in the mid-2010s and connects instrumented trees across research and public sites.

Sap-flow sensors, dendrometers and local weather instruments register otherwise imperceptible changes in water transport, growth and stress. Selected measurements are translated into web updates and first-person social-media posts. A tree thereby appears to report heat, drought, recovery or daily rhythms, while the scientific measurements remain available as the basis for the communication.
publics_text: The project operates through instrumented forests, parks and school or university sites, with a distributed online presence rather than a single exhibition (**D**). Scientists and technicians are participating publics; students, teachers, park visitors and online followers are encountered publics. Forestry and municipal land-management organisations are potentially decision-capable. Living trees are sensed participants, although humans determine what is measured and said.
rq1: Tree physiology unfolds internally and at temporal scales that do not align with casual observation. Specialist data can remain inaccessible even when it directly concerns public experiences of heat and drought.
rq2: Tactics include long-duration sensing, scientific visualisation, first-person personification, social distribution and emplacement in familiar public landscapes.
rq3: The first-person voice makes data legible but can imply intentional speech. Sensor selection privileges measurable processes and platform algorithms influence who encounters the posts. Following or liking a tree is evidence of attention, not of altered forestry practice or climate action.
evaluation: A stronger epistemic bridge than pure role-play, but public action and platform afterlife are uncertain.
configuration: Hidden physiological change → continuous sensing plus tree-authored social voice → scientific, educational and online publics → documented measurements and circulation → ventriloquism, metric/platform and action-gap tensions → keep the translation chain visible and connect alerts to care decisions.
evidence_boundary: Strong for instrumentation and communication design; uneven for public interpretation, behavioural consequence and institutional adoption. Sources: [TreeWatch.net](https://treewatch.net/) and [`portfolio/treewatch.md`](../../portfolio/treewatch.md).
format: physiological sensing and social-media status

csv.rq2: Sap-flow and dendrometer data, real-time modelling and personified posts.
csv.rq3: Instrument-grounded signals still require human-authored interpretation; platform dependence threatens continuity.

title: The Art of Listening: Under Water
creators: Jana Winderen with Tony Myatt
occasions: Art Basel Miami Beach 2019; Lenfest Center, Columbia 2022
publics: Art-fair/gallery listeners, sound-art and marine-ecology publics
summary:
*Art Listening Under Water* is a spatial sound installation by Jana Winderen with sound designer Tony Myatt. It was presented in 2019 in connection with Art Basel Miami Beach and later at the Lenfest Center for the Arts in New York in 2022.

Hydrophone recordings place listeners inside an acoustic field of underwater animals, ice, currents and human-generated noise. Rather than turning the recordings into a visual dashboard, the work preserves sound as sound and redistributes the audible range through a carefully composed loudspeaker environment. It asks audiences to encounter an inhabited ocean that ordinary human listening and land-based attention exclude.
publics_text: Documented presentations include Miami Beach in 2019 and Columbia University’s Lenfest Center in 2022 (**D**). Encountered publics include contemporary-art, sound-art, university and marine-environment audiences. The animals and habitats are recorded rather than present. Marine researchers and conservation organisations are interpretive allies, while shipping, fisheries and regulators are relevant but not demonstrably reached decision-capable publics.
rq1: Underwater life is physically remote and often drowned out in public discourse by visual representations. Anthropogenic noise is also difficult to perceive from land.
rq2: The work uses hydrophone field recording, spatial composition, low-frequency embodiment, darkness and within-modal amplification. It does not pretend to translate sound into a humanlike language.
rq3: Composition necessarily selects locations, species and intensities. Aesthetic immersion can make ecological disturbance affectively present, but it can also detach recordings from the infrastructures and jurisdictions producing the noise. Ticketed art access and the absence of an action pathway constrain political reach.
evaluation: Excellent non-visual translation; weak evidence of action beyond listening.
configuration: Inaudible and remote underwater relations → hydrophone recording and spatial audition → gallery/university listening public → documented presentations, interpretation outcomes unknown → compositional authority, aestheticisation and access tensions → retain acoustic specificity while naming sites, causes and response routes.
evidence_boundary: Strong for authorship, medium and presentation; limited for audience research or conservation consequences. Sources: [Jana Winderen’s project documentation](https://www.janawinderen.com/exhibitions/the-art-of-listening-under-water) and [`portfolio/art-of-listening-under-water.md`](../../portfolio/art-of-listening-under-water.md).
format: immersive multichannel sound installation

csv.rq2: Hydrophone field recording, sound-to-sound amplification, spatial audio and gallery restaging.
csv.rq3: Aesthetic immersion may beautify crisis and edit whole ecosystems into an authored composition.

title: The Sound of Light in Trees
creators: David Dunn
occasions: Field recording; album/CD and online circulation
publics: Sound-art listeners, forest scientists/managers, affected forest communities
summary:
*The Sound of Light in Trees* is a sound work by David Dunn, first published in 2006 and subsequently reissued. It emerged from field recordings of bark beetles and other organisms made with custom microphones and probes placed in or against trees.

Dunn’s recordings reveal clicks, pulses and granular textures produced inside bark and wood. The album makes a sub-bark acoustic world available to listeners who would otherwise encounter a forest mainly at human scale. Its title also destabilises sensory categories: what appears visually as light, tree and landscape becomes an internally active acoustic habitat.
publics_text: The work has circulated through recordings, radio, talks and sound-art contexts rather than a single stable exhibition (**D/secondary**). Encountered publics include experimental-music listeners, acoustic ecologists, entomologists and forest researchers. Forest managers form a possible decision-capable public. Bark beetles and trees are recorded participants but have no role in the later framing or circulation.
rq1: Life beneath bark is spatially concealed and temporally difficult to follow. Public accounts of bark beetles often reduce them to a visible outbreak or threat after complex interactions are already under way.
rq2: Tactics include probe-microphone invention, patient field listening, minimally recognisable acoustic composition and album-based circulation beyond the recording site.
rq3: Amplification can complicate the image of a silent tree, but interpretation can still fold beetles into a threat narrative. The recording apparatus and the composer determine what counts as signal. Claims that listening changes forestry intervention require evidence beyond the artwork’s documented circulation.
evaluation: A durable sonic artifact and strong epistemic case, with unresolved activist causality.
configuration: Concealed sub-bark life → custom contact/probe recording → sound-art and forest-science publics → durable recording archive → selection, pest-framing and action-gap tensions → contextualise species relations and distinguish auditory discovery from management impact.
evidence_boundary: Strong for the recording work and its scientific-artistic method; limited for public-response and management outcomes. Sources: [artist release documentation](https://daviddunn.bandcamp.com/album/the-sound-of-light-in-trees) and [`portfolio/sound-of-light-in-trees.md`](../../portfolio/sound-of-light-in-trees.md).
format: bioacoustic field recording and album

csv.rq2: Probe microphones, within-modal amplification, album circulation and field-science collaboration.
csv.rq3: Recording can frame beetles primarily as threats; claimed management consequences are creator-reported and need independent evidence.

title: The Hive
creators: Wolfgang Buttress, BDP, Simmonds Studio, Stage One, BE Collective
occasions: UK Pavilion, Expo Milano 2015; Royal Botanic Gardens Kew
publics: Expo and botanic-garden visitors, design/media publics, beekeepers; managed colony
summary:
*The Hive* is an immersive architectural installation commissioned as the United Kingdom Pavilion for Expo Milano 2015. It was designed by Wolfgang Buttress with BDP, Simmonds Studio, Stage One and a wider scientific and production team, and was reconstructed at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, in 2016.

A lattice structure resembling a vast swarm surrounds visitors with light and sound. Signals from a living honeybee colony modulate the installation, creating a remote coupling between colony activity and the public environment. The project combines architecture, telemetry and spectacle to make collective insect life perceptible at human scale.
publics_text: The work was encountered by international-expo visitors in Milan and later by garden, family, tourist and educational publics at Kew (**D/CR**). Beekeepers, scientists, engineers and garden staff are participating and maintenance publics. A live colony supplies data but is geographically separate from visitors. Agricultural and biodiversity institutions are relevant decision-capable publics; reach to them should not be assumed from visitor volume.
rq1: Colony processes are spatially hidden, distributed across thousands of bees and difficult to apprehend through an individual-animal frame. Specialist monitoring alone does not make those processes publicly meaningful.
rq2: Tactics include monumental architecture, live telemetry, responsive LEDs, sound composition, biomimetic form, family-accessible immersion and reinstallation at a major public garden.
rq3: Spectacle delivers reach but may turn colony complexity into ambience. Honeybees’ cultural charisma can eclipse wild pollinator diversity and agricultural politics. Visitor numbers show exposure, not interpretation or changed practice. Continuous data and a rebuilt pavilion also depend on substantial technical and care labour.
evaluation: An exceptional reach/decay case, but not evidence of pollinator benefit.
configuration: Hidden collective insect activity → live-data architectural spectacle → expo and botanic-garden publics → very high documented exposure, thinner engagement evidence → charisma, spectacle and maintenance tensions → pair sensory scale with pollinator plurality and evaluated action pathways.
evidence_boundary: Strong for commissioning, technical form and public presentation; weaker for what visitors learned or did afterwards. Sources: [Stage One project documentation](https://www.stageone.co.uk/projects/the-hive/) and [`portfolio/the-hive.md`](../../portfolio/the-hive.md).
format: architectural pavilion driven by live hive vibration

csv.rq2: Live accelerometer feed, LEDs, soundscape, architectural spectacle and permanent reinstallation.

title: Nukabot
creators: Dominique Chen and Ferment Media Research collaborators
occasions: Triennale di Milano; 2121 DESIGN SIGHT; Miraikan; other design venues
publics: Museum/design visitors, fermentation practitioners, cultural publics; microbial community
summary:
*Nukabot* is a family of fermented-food interfaces developed from 2019 onward by Dominique Chen and Ferment Media Research collaborators. Credits vary by iteration: the 2021 publication includes Chen, Young ah Seong, Hiraku Ogura, Yuto Mitani, Naoto Sekiya and Kiichi Moriya; the 2024 publication includes Chen, Youngah Seong and Kazuhiro Jo. Its central artefact is a sensor-equipped rice-bran fermentation vessel that communicates conditions relevant to microbial care.

Japanese nukadoko fermentation requires repeated mixing, smelling, tasting and adjustment. *Nukabot* senses environmental and biochemical conditions and produces conversational prompts or vocal expressions that invite a carer to respond. It does not merely display microbial data; it locates computation inside a culturally familiar, ongoing practice of reciprocal maintenance.
publics_text: Iterations have appeared in design, media-art and science venues in Japan, including Triennale-related, 21_21 DESIGN SIGHT and Miraikan contexts, alongside academic demonstrations (**D/CR; verify venue-year pairing before publication**). Participating publics include researchers, designers, fermenters and household carers. Museum visitors are encountered publics. Microbial communities are living participants whose conditions are sensed, but humans author the interface and consume its products.
rq1: Microbial activity is invisible and care knowledge is sensory, tacit and temporally distributed. A one-off exhibit struggles to convey this duration.
rq2: The work uses a familiar vessel, chemical/environmental sensing, conversational voice, humour and repeated care routines. Cultural familiarity bridges expert microbiology and domestic practice.
rq3: Voice can sustain attention but implies an integrated microbial speaker where a multispecies community and technical model exist. Sensor values may displace embodied knowledge even as the project celebrates it. The microbes’ flourishing remains entangled with human taste, food production and eventual consumption.
evaluation: A valuable long-duration care case if voice and metabolism are kept analytically separate.
configuration: Invisible microbial transformation → situated sensing and conversational care → household/design/museum publics → documented prototypes and exhibitions → ventriloquism, cultural-translation and instrumental-care tensions → make model limits and human–microbial reciprocity explicit.
evidence_boundary: Strong for concept and prototype; presentation chronology and public-response claims require final cross-check against each credited iteration. In Ikeya, Barati and Wensveen's 2025 review, *Nukabot* appears as visual exemplar **○6**, source-local reference **[39]**, with image credit **© Dominique Chen**; these numbers are retained as provenance for the supplied visual reference rather than treated as this portfolio's numbering. Sources: [ACM CHI 2021 DOI](https://doi.org/10.1145/3411763.3451605), [`portfolio/nukabot.md`](../../portfolio/nukabot.md) and [`references/ikeya2025aesthetics.md`](../ikeya2025aesthetics.md).
format: sensorised fermentation vessel with voice interface

title: The Great Animal Orchestra
creators: Bernie Krause and United Visual Artists
occasions: Fondation Cartier; Peabody Essex Museum; Exploratorium; international tour
publics: Ticketed museum visitors, sound-art/science publics; recorded ecosystems represented
summary:
*The Great Animal Orchestra* is an immersive installation developed by bioacoustician Bernie Krause with United Visual Artists. It was commissioned by Fondation Cartier pour l’art contemporain in 2016 from Krause’s long-term archive of habitat recordings.

Panoramic spectrograms move in synchrony with multichannel soundscapes recorded across habitats. Visitors hear biophony as patterned ecological organisation and can visually follow acoustic niches, absences and transformations. The installation makes a scientific archive sensorially navigable while framing soundscape loss as evidence of environmental change.
publics_text: First presented at Fondation Cartier in Paris in 2016, the installation has toured and entered museum and science-centre contexts, including the Peabody Essex Museum and Exploratorium (**D**). Encountered publics include art, natural-history, science-centre and educational audiences. Krause and institutional teams are participating publics; recorded animal communities and habitats are represented participants, not live ones. Conservation institutions are potential decision-capable publics.
rq1: Ecological degradation can occur acoustically before it becomes visually obvious, while distant habitats remain outside most people’s experience. A specialist archive does not automatically become a public encounter.
rq2: Tactics include long-term field recording, an archive spanning locations and decades, multichannel immersion, synchronised spectrograms, narrative comparison and international touring.
rq3: A beautiful museum environment can make disappearance intensely felt, yet also aestheticise it. Curatorial selection gives coherence to disparate habitats and may obscure Indigenous territories, local conflicts and recording conditions. Attendance evidences exposure rather than conservation action.
evaluation: A major public bridge between scientific archive and affect, not a demonstrated conservation intervention.
configuration: Remote and vanishing biophony → archive plus audiovisual immersion → international museum/science public → documented touring and repeat presentation → aestheticisation, territorial context and action-gap tensions → attach each soundscape to situated ecological and governance histories.
evidence_boundary: Strong for artistic form and exhibition history; limited public-outcome and conservation-impact evaluation. Sources: [Fondation Cartier project page](https://www.fondationcartier.com/en/exhibitions/the-great-animal-orchestra) and [`portfolio/great-animal-orchestra.md`](../../portfolio/great-animal-orchestra.md).
format: immersive audio-visual museum installation
