csv.rq2: Field-recording archive, spectrogram-light translation, reflective architecture and international touring.
csv.rq3: Museum beauty can turn disappearance into contemplative spectacle; access is ticketed and action outcomes are unknown.

title: Ghost Forest
creators: Maya Lin; Madison Square Park Conservancy
entity: Dead Atlantic white cedars and climate-stressed forests
occasions: Madison Square Park, New York, May–November 2021
publics: Park passers-by, art/climate publics, local organisations; source forests implicated
summary:
*Ghost Forest* was a public installation by Maya Lin presented by Madison Square Park Conservancy in New York from May to November 2021. It comprised forty-nine Atlantic white cedar trees killed by saltwater intrusion and sourced from New Jersey’s Pine Barrens.

The standing dead trees abruptly changed a familiar urban park into an image of forest loss. Sound components and related public programmes connected the installation to threatened habitats, climate change and local ecological action. Because the trees were materially present rather than represented by images, visitors encountered both monumentality and decay over months.
publics_text: The principal site was Madison Square Park, a free civic space traversed by commuters, residents, tourists, school groups and art audiences (**D**). Forestry and conservation partners, educators and park staff were participating publics. The source forest and communities affected by coastal change constitute affected publics. City, park and climate organisations are potential decision-capable publics. The dead cedars are material witnesses, not living collaborators.
rq1: Forest die-off is geographically distributed and can remain abstract to city publics. Climate causality is difficult to infer from an individual dead tree without contextual explanation.
rq2: Tactics include material relocation, monumental repetition, free civic siting, duration, sound, education and public programming.
rq3: Moving dead trees produces a forceful public witness but detaches them from the source ecosystem. Monumental spectacle can individualise “climate change” while saltwater intrusion, land management and environmental inequality require specific accounts. Transport, installation and post-exhibition material afterlife are part of the work’s politics.
evaluation: A powerful material witness with a clearer civic pathway than most climate spectacles.
configuration: Distant distributed forest death → relocated cedar monument in a daily urban route → broad civic public → sustained exposure and programme participation → displacement, carbon/logistics and causal-simplification tensions → document sourcing, afterlife and locally actionable climate relations.
evidence_boundary: Strong for dates, material composition and programming; limited for longitudinal public action. Sources: [Madison Square Park Conservancy project page](https://madisonsquarepark.org/art/exhibitions/maya-lin-ghost-forest/) and [`portfolio/ghost-forest.md`](../../portfolio/ghost-forest.md).

title: Particle Falls
creators: Andrea Polli with Chuck Varga
occasions: ZERO1/01SJ 2010; Philadelphia Sensing Change; later redeployments
publics: Street passers-by, residents, arts/science publics, pollution-affected communities
summary:
*Particle Falls* is a public artwork by Andrea Polli and Chuck Varga, first realised in 2010. It uses a nephelometer or comparable air-quality sensor to convert changing particulate levels into a large real-time projection on an urban façade.

The projection resembles a luminous waterfall. When airborne particulate concentration rises, visual disruptions appear in the falling field. Passing traffic and local conditions therefore become immediately associated with a changing public image. The work transforms ambient exposure from a numerical report into a shared street event.
publics_text: Documented installations include San Jose during the 2010 ZERO1 context and Philadelphia in 2013, with later versions in other cities (**D/secondary**). Encountered publics include pedestrians, commuters, residents and festival visitors. People living or working near the sensor are affected publics, while public-health departments, transport planners and municipal officials are decision-capable publics. Air and particulate matter are sensed material actors.
rq1: Particulate pollution is invisible in ordinary experience and often encountered through delayed regional statistics that obscure local peaks and unequal exposure.
rq2: Tactics include real-time sensing, monumental public projection, intuitive visual change, street-level placement and a direct link between local activity and display.
rq3: A single sensor produces a highly local account whose calibration and siting matter. Visibility may create concern without identifying responsibility or enabling action. The aesthetically attractive waterfall can make pollution watchable while communities continue to bear exposure.
evaluation: A strong civic-sensing bridge with plausible immediacy but little evidence of policy effect.
configuration: Invisible local particulate exposure → live façade visualisation → street and environmental-health public → documented urban installations → sensor-siting, aestheticisation and action-gap tensions → publish measurement limits and connect display to health and transport decisions.

title: Squeeker: The Mouse Coach
creators: Jiabao Li
occasions: IDFA DocLab 2023; Ars Electronica 2024; TEI 2026
publics: Festival/app publics, runners, lab-animal issue publics; live mouse affected
summary:
*Squeeker: The Mouse Coach* is a 2023–present project by Jiabao Li and collaborators. It combines a live mouse, an exercise wheel, a mobile running interface, documentary media and later research framing; versions were shown at IDFA DocLab in 2023, Ars Electronica in 2024 and an ACM TEI context in 2026.

A human runner follows exercise prompts linked to a mouse’s wheel activity, reversing the familiar laboratory arrangement in which mice perform for human observation. The mouse becomes a charismatic “coach,” and humour makes experimental power relations easy to grasp. App and film components extend the encounter beyond the live apparatus.
publics_text: Documented contexts span immersive-documentary, media-art and research venues (**D**). Encountered publics include festival visitors, app users, runners, designers and animal–computer interaction researchers. Participating publics include the mouse, handlers, the production team and human runners. Animal-care personnel and venue ethics structures are decision-capable for the live animal, while laboratory institutions form the wider issue public.
rq1: Laboratory animals’ repetitive labour and asymmetrical relation to research systems usually remain hidden. Animal experimentation is also polarised in public discourse, making sustained reflection difficult.
rq2: The work uses role reversal, humour, cross-species synchronisation, bodily exercise, a charismatic individual animal, documentary narrative and distribution across app, film and installation.
rq3: Calling the mouse a coach symbolically redistributes authority, but the human team still designs the enclosure, interprets the activity and controls circulation. A visible live animal generates ethical immediacy while also becoming an exhibition apparatus. Publicly available project records do not by themselves establish a complete welfare protocol or the mouse’s freedom to disengage.
evaluation: Provocative but ethically high-risk; retain as a critical case, not a success exemplar.
configuration: Hidden laboratory hierarchy → comic mouse–human role reversal → festival, running and ACI publics → documented presentations and interactions → symbolic-agency, welfare and apparatus tensions → publish care, rest, withdrawal and decision protocols alongside the work.
evidence_boundary: Strong for concept and presentation trajectory; welfare conditions and audience consequences need project-team or venue documentation before stronger claims. title: The Elephant in the Room
creators: Jiabao Li with legal, NGO, performance and media collaborators
entity: Captive Asian elephants and animal entertainment
medium: AR; interactive 3D; drone sound; music video; campaign
occasions: Online campaign; 28 March 2024 appellate hearing context; press circulation
publics: Online supporters, animal-rights issue publics, lawyers/NGOs, courts/authorities, tourists; elephants affected
summary:
*The Elephant in the Room* is a 2024 activist media project directed by Jiabao Li, developed with legal, NGO, performance, music, cinematography and drone collaborators. It addressed captive Asian-elephant training and performance at Wild Elephant Valley in Yunnan in conjunction with a public-interest lawsuit.

An interactive three-dimensional elephant bears clickable scars that link visible wounds to alleged tools and training practices. An augmented-reality mode places a life-size elephant in the viewer’s room and invites screenshots under the lawsuit hashtag. During the 28 March 2024 court hearing, user interactions were linked to drones emitting elephant distress sounds near the court. A companion music and dance video rewrote a familiar cartoon song and used contortion to embody forced performance postures.
publics_text: This was a networked campaign and court-adjacent intervention rather than a conventional gallery exhibition (**D/CR/contested**). Participating publics included the artist team, lawyers, NGOs, online supporters and performers. Encountered publics included social-media users, press readers and tourism audiences. Captive elephants are the affected public; the court, tourism operator and wildlife authorities are decision-capable publics. The elephants did not directly control the representation.
rq1: Training violence is hidden behind entertainment, rescue and conservation branding. Visitors encounter spectacular behaviours without seeing how they are produced, while legal responsibility remains institutionally difficult to access.
rq2: Tactics include scar-linked evidence, life-size AR, a screenshot/hashtag invitation, drone sound, an emotionally legible 3D figure, a nostalgic song remix, bodily performance and alignment with litigation.
rq3: The project is unusually valuable because its public success narrative is contested. The creator page states that Wild Elephant Valley cancelled elephant performances as a result of the campaign. The publicly reported appellate outcome of 16 May 2024 states that the appeal was dismissed and the lower judgment upheld. These records do not establish that the artwork caused a change in performances. Lawyers, NGOs, artists, operators and courts also act as competing human proxies for elephants, with unequal authority to define welfare, evidence and remedy.
evaluation: Essential RQ3 case precisely because its causal success narrative conflicts with the public legal record; include only with explicit correction.
configuration: Hidden training violence and conservation branding → evidentiary AR, viral music and court-adjacent sound → online advocacy, tourism and legal publics → documented campaign and hearing, disputed downstream result → causal-attribution and proxy-authority tensions → retain as a core critical case with creator claim and court record visibly separated.
evidence_boundary: Strong for the media components and campaign claims; the legal record contradicts any simple victory account, and no causal inference is warranted. Sources: [creator project page](https://www.jiabaoli.org/elephant-in-the-room), [Yunnan High People’s Court/Xinhua report, 16 May 2024](https://www.yn.xinhuanet.com/20240516/1608c066a947408a8672dac2174d14ed/c.html) and [`data/jiabao_work_normalization.md`](../../data/jiabao_work_normalization.md).

title: OctoNation
creators: OctoNation, founded by Warren Carlyle
occasions: Online platforms, classrooms, aquarium/science and public outreach
publics: Smartphone learners, enthusiasts, educators, scientists, photographers, aquarists; octopuses represented
summary:
*OctoNation* is a nonprofit octopus-education community founded by Warren Carlyle in 2015. It is not a Jiabao Li project. It is included as a reach-oriented comparator because it brings specialist cephalopod knowledge into social-media, educational and popular-science settings.

The organisation circulates vivid underwater imagery, accessible research summaries, humour, recurring octopus characters and expert commentary. It turns unusual anatomy, behaviour and individual stories into serial content that can be shared without first entering a museum or scientific institution. Its bridge is therefore infrastructural and editorial: sustained platform presence rather than a bounded artefact.
publics_text: Public occasions include social-media channels, online community activity, educational materials, classes, campaigns and collaborations with scientists and underwater photographers (**D/CR**). Encountered publics include casual platform users, families and marine-life enthusiasts. Educators, scientists, photographers, aquarists and moderators are participating publics. Conservation organisations and ocean-policy actors are possible decision-capable publics. Octopuses are represented through footage and scientific interpretation.
rq1: Cephalopod science remains specialist, while fear-based or catastrophic conservation messages often fail to retain attention in crowded platform environments.
rq2: Tactics include species charisma, episodic storytelling, humour, vivid imagery, shareable facts, named individuals, repeated contact and collaboration with recognised experts.
rq3: The same platform grammar that expands reach can turn octopuses into branded content. Follower counts and views demonstrate exposure, not comprehension or conservation action. Editorial curation, sponsorship, moderation and platform algorithms shape which species and facts become visible. Charismatic octopuses may also eclipse less photogenic marine relations.
evaluation: A high-value reach comparator, not Jiabao's work and not yet evidence that viral affection becomes ocean action.
configuration: Specialist marine knowledge and weak attention → serial charismatic social storytelling → mass, educational and expert-linked online publics → strong circulation evidence, limited action evidence → platform, branding and charisma tensions → analyse reach separately from conservation consequence.
evidence_boundary: Strong for organisational history and communication format; outcome claims are mainly self-reported and should not be treated as independent conservation evaluation. Source: [OctoNation’s official history](https://shop.octonation.com/pages/about-us).

title: Ice Watch
creators: Olafur Eliasson and Minik Rosing
entity: Greenlandic glacial ice and climate time
medium: Twelve ice blocks in civic space
occasions: Copenhagen City Hall Square; Paris Place du Panthéon; Tate/Bloomberg London
publics: Passers-by, climate/COP publics, museum/corporate-district visitors, media; Greenlandic landscapes implicated
summary:
*Ice Watch* is a public climate installation by Olafur Eliasson and geologist Minik Rosing. Twelve blocks of Greenlandic glacial ice were arranged like a clock in Copenhagen in 2014, Paris in 2015 and London in 2018.

Visitors could touch, smell, listen to and watch ancient ice melt in real time. The work brought a material fragment of the Greenland ice sheet into civic space and converted planetary-scale, statistically described change into a bodily and durational encounter. The clock formation linked melting matter to the limited time for climate response.
publics_text: The installations took place at Copenhagen City Hall Square from 26–29 October 2014, Place du Panthéon in Paris from 3–13 December 2015 during COP21, and outside Tate Modern/Bloomberg in London from 11 December 2018 to 2 January 2019 (**D**). Free public siting reached passersby, tourists, school groups, art audiences, journalists, activists and climate-conference publics. Climate negotiators and municipal/cultural institutions were decision-capable publics. Greenlandic ice was materially present; Greenlandic communities were not automatically represented by it.
rq1: Arctic melting is geographically remote, represented through models and aggregates, and temporally difficult to feel. Climate communication must bridge distance without pretending that one object contains the whole crisis.
rq2: Tactics include actual glacial material, touch, sound, smell, visible melting, clock-like arrangement, prominent civic placement, repeat staging and alignment with IPCC/COP moments.
rq3: Extracting and transporting ice introduces carbon, logistical and symbolic costs. A universal “humanity and climate” framing can mute Greenlandic sovereignty, uneven responsibility and the political economy of emissions. The trace of melting is incontrovertible as an encounter but does not demonstrate policy influence or durable behavioural change.
evaluation: A canonical embodied-climate bridge and highly retellable work, but awareness and policy effects must not be inferred.
configuration: Remote statistical climate change → touchable ancient ice melting in civic time → mass street, museum and COP-adjacent publics → documented large exposure and press circulation → footprint, sovereignty and awareness/action tensions → publish logistics and connect universal affect to differentiated responsibility.
evidence_boundary: Excellent documentation of dates, locations, materials and intent; no basis for inferring policy effect from visibility. Source: [official *Ice Watch* archive](https://olafureliasson.net/artwork/ice-watch-2014/).

format: public installation of twelve ice blocks

title: Synplant
creators: Youyang Hu, Chiaochi Chou, Yasuaki Kakehi
occasions: ZOU-NO-HANA Futurescape 2022; Ars Electronica Garden 2023; Xlab and art presentations
publics: Art/technology festival visitors, HCI audiences; instrumented plants
summary:
*Synplant* (2022) is an installation by Youyang Hu, Chiaochi Chou and Yasuaki Kakehi. It combines multiple living plants with bioelectrical sensing, machine-learning analysis, sound, light and cymatic water patterns.

The installation exposes plants to wind and rain-like stimuli, measures bioelectrical activity and classifies signal patterns. These classifications drive audiovisual events across a field of machine–plant hybrids. Visitors encounter a distributed environment in which plant response, weather simulation, water vibration and computational interpretation are intertwined.
publics_text: Documented presentations include ZOU-NO-HANA Futurescape in Yokohama (2022), the Xlab showcase *Ways of Uninventing* in Tokyo (2023) and the Ars Electronica Garden Tokyo contribution to *Who Owns the Truth?* in Linz (2023), alongside the SIGGRAPH 2023 Art Papers publication (**D**). Encountered publics include art-festival, design-research and technology audiences. The artists, laboratories and technicians are participating publics. Living plants are sensed participants, but training and classification remain human-controlled.
rq1: Plant–environment interaction is electrophysiological, distributed and invisible to gallery visitors. Raw data offers little access without a perceptual bridge.
rq2: Tactics include plant electrophysiology, supervised classification, environmental stimulation, spatialised sound/light and cymatic water patterns in an immersive multi-unit field.
rq3: The official framing describes a plant “perspective,” but a learned classification and aesthetic mapping are not equivalent to botanical experience. Training labels, sensor placement and output design decide which changes become legible. The work opens an epistemic relation while risking the conversion of uncertainty into a confident voice.
evaluation: A strong new epistemic case with exhibition evidence, but interpretation and public-effect validation remain limited.
configuration: Invisible plant response → sensing, classification and cymatic audiovisual field → art/technology/research publics → documented exhibitions and publication → model-authority and perspective-claim tensions → disclose labels, error and alternative interpretations.

title: Eye of Flora / Immersive Flora

summary:
*Eye of Flora* is a 2024–ongoing series by Youyang Hu, Cyprien Fol, Chiaochi Chou, Verena Griess and Yasuaki Kakehi, with collaborations spanning the University of Tokyo, ETH Zurich and National Tsing Hua University. *Immersive Flora* is the related virtual-reality iteration.

Living-plant electrophysiology is combined with three-dimensional forest reconstruction, AI analysis and particle visualisation. Plant-derived signals animate digital agents and environments, allowing a visitor to move through an MR/VR forest that remains coupled to living organisms. The series explicitly responds to the prospect of digital forests that omit actual trees.
publics_text: Documented contexts include CHI Interactivity and SIGGRAPH Asia Art Papers in 2024, the ETH AI Center’s AI+X Summit in Zurich, Climate Imaginarium in New York, Xlab’s *Well-tangled* showcase in Tokyo, the 2024–25 *AI·Human·Multiverse* context in Gwangju and Hu’s *Being Transducer* exhibition at Pace University Art Gallery (**D; individual versions vary by venue**). Encountered publics include XR, AI, media-art, university and gallery audiences. Living plants, researchers and technical teams participate; forest ecologies are partly recorded or reconstructed.

rq2: Tactics include electrophysiology, AI analysis, digital twins, 3D capture, mixed-reality co-presence, aesthetic particles and circulation across research and public-art venues.
rq3: The “digital plant agent” is produced through human-selected sensors, models and graphics. Saying it shares unseen responses risks collapsing data, proxy and voice. High-tech mediation may also centre computational novelty over forest-specific histories or material care.
evaluation: An important bridge between ecological sensing and virtual environments; retain with a mediation disclosure.
configuration: Plant absence from virtual forests → live biosignal–digital-twin coupling → XR/AI/gallery publics → documented research and exhibitions → data-as-voice, novelty and ecological-context tensions → preserve the living linkage and expose the computational translation chain.

title: Forest Resonance
creators: Youyang Hu and six collaborators
occasions: Forest-therapy pilot in Japan; DIS 2026 demonstration

summary:
*Forest Resonance* is a 2026 demonstration by Youyang Hu, Yating Dai, Shin Chen, Yumi Nishihara, Junji Watanabe, Yasue Kishino and Yasuaki Kakehi. It is a portable sonic-haptic field system designed to augment free movement in a forest.

The system senses environmental vibration, electrical conductivity and plant bioelectrical activity, then translates selected signals into sound and haptic feedback carried by a visitor. A pilot was conducted in a Japanese forest-therapy context. Unlike a gallery reconstruction, the device attempts to keep attention situated among the substrates and organisms being sensed.
publics_text: At the time of this appendix, the work is documented as a DIS 2026 companion-proceedings demonstration and pilot rather than a mature touring installation (**D**). Participants include researchers, forest-therapy facilitators and pilot users. Forest organisms and substrates are sensed participants. Wider publics, land stewards and health or forestry institutions remain prospective rather than demonstrated.
rq1: Subtle vibration, conductivity and bioelectric change are missed during ordinary forest visits, including guided wellness encounters that may reproduce a generic idea of “nature.”
rq2: Tactics include portable multi-sensing, wearable sound and haptics, free walking and in-situ augmentation rather than visual substitution.
rq3: Instrument selection defines what counts as forest “resonance.” A short demonstration and pilot cannot establish ecological attunement, therapeutic benefit or care. Wearable feedback may redirect attention toward the device and treat living signals as a personalised experience resource.
evaluation: Promising non-visual in-situ tactic, currently a watchlist prototype rather than a proven public work.
configuration: Subtle in-situ forest processes → portable sonic-haptic translation → pilot/research/therapy public → early demonstration evidence → metric-selection and wellness-instrumentalisation tensions → retain as a watchlist prototype pending longer field evaluation.
evidence_boundary: Early-stage evidence only; no claim of established public or ecological outcome. Source: [DIS 2026 companion programme](https://dis.acm.org/2026/companion-proceedings/).

summary:
*House Pond Project* is an ongoing practice begun in 2025 by Youyang Hu, Kuan-Ju Wu, Chiaochi Chou and Yasuaki Kakehi. It constructs a sensor-equipped pond ecosystem within domestic living space.

Water, plants, electronic devices and embedded sensors form a living interface that can register changes and encounters among people, animals and other organisms. The pond is intended to attract nonhuman visitors indoors and accumulate a long-term archive of ecological transformation. Its central wager is not a brief representation but a continuing obligation of cohabitation.
publics_text: The work was presented as *Sensus Pond* in the 2025 Xlab *We Matter* showcase in Tokyo and connected to an IASDR 2025 pictorial, while its main site remains a domestic ecology (**D**). Household residents, designers and researchers are participating publics. Exhibition visitors are encountered publics. Plants, water and visiting species are living participants. Building managers, animal-health professionals and local ecological authorities may become decision-capable where care or escape risks arise.

rq2: Tactics include living habitat construction, invitation rather than representation, embedded sensing, domestic scale, longitudinal observation and a water-based interface.

evaluation: Conceptually strong for cohabitation and afterlife, but too early for outcome claims.

title: Pollution Pods
creators: Michael Pinsky with the Climart collaboration
entity: Urban atmospheres, air pollution and climate-linked ecologies
occasions: Trondheim public park; Somerset House; WHO/UN and international festival circulation
publics: Park and cultural visitors, climate/health publics, researchers and policy-facing audiences; pollution-burdened communities represented
summary:
*Pollution Pods* is an environmental artwork created by Michael Pinsky through the Climart collaboration and commissioned by the Norwegian University of Science and Technology. First exhibited in 2017, it consists of five connected geodesic domes that simulate atmospheric conditions associated with a Norwegian coastal location and London, New Delhi, Beijing and São Paulo.

Visitors walk through a sequence that shifts from cool, clean coastal air toward increasingly hot, humid, smoky or scented environments. Safe substances, temperature and humidity produce a bodily analogy of unequal urban pollution without exposing visitors to the actual harmful gases. The circular route makes atmospheric difference sequential and inhaled rather than statistical. Its iconic architecture also works as a visible recruitment device before the visitor enters.
publics_text: The first evaluated presentations were in a public park in Trondheim and at Somerset House in London (**D**). The work subsequently circulated through health, climate, art and policy-facing events, including WHO- and UN-linked contexts (**D/CR**). A published questionnaire study covers 2,662 visitors at the first two sites (**D**). Encountered publics include park passers-by, cultural visitors, climate and health publics, researchers and political delegates. Residents who routinely breathe the represented pollution are affected publics but were not equivalent participants in the evaluated encounters.
rq1: Air pollution is ambient and unequally distributed, while climate change is often communicated through remote numbers. People in cleaner-air locations cannot ordinarily encounter the atmospheric burden attached to other cities, and information alone competes poorly for public attention.
rq2: The work uses full-body sequential simulation, smell, heat, humidity, architectural spectacle, public-park siting, international touring and embedded psychological evaluation. It turns breathing—normally unnoticed—into the unavoidable medium of comparison.
rq3: The domes offer a safe, authored simulation, not transported urban air, and can blur the distinction between toxic pollutants and mostly odourless greenhouse gases. The itinerary also risks turning unequal exposure into temporary cultural consumption by comparatively mobile visitors. In the 2,662-person study, intentions increased only very slightly (reported effect size *d* = 0.07); just 2% of installation visitors joined the offered action platform, and behavioural uptake could not be detected. Strong reach and emotion therefore did not establish an action bridge.
evaluation: A rare large-public artwork with unusually strong evaluation evidence; its failed action bridge is as important as its immersive reach.
configuration: Remote and unequal atmospheric harm → inhaled multisensory itinerary plus iconic public architecture → park, art, health and policy-facing publics → large documented exposure and very small intention change → simulation, inequality and intention–behaviour tensions → pair spectacle with locally accountable action routes and valid follow-up measures.
evidence_boundary: Strong for form, first venues and immediate visitor response; unusually strong negative evidence for behavioural uptake; no basis for claiming lasting change. Sources: [artist project page](https://www.michaelpinsky.com/portfolio/pollution-pods-2/), [Cape Farewell circulation record](https://www.capefarewell.com/pollution-pods/) and [Sommer et al. evaluation](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gloenvcha.2019.101992).

title: The Substitute
creators: Alexandra Daisy Ginsberg with The Mill and scientific collaborators
entity: Northern white rhinoceros, extinction and technological resurrection
medium: Paired life-size video and sound installation
occasions: Cooper Hewitt Design Triennial; FACT Liverpool; Onassis Stegi; natural-history museums; Biennale of Sydney
publics: Museum, biennial, design, AI and conservation publics; extinct rhinos represented
summary:
*The Substitute* is Alexandra Daisy Ginsberg’s 2019 paired video-and-sound installation, produced with The Mill, with behaviour informed by DeepMind research and rare northern white rhinoceros footage supplied by Richard Policht. It was commissioned by Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum and Cube design museum and entered Cooper Hewitt’s permanent collection.

A five-metre life-size projection presents a digital northern white rhino learning the limits of an empty virtual room. Its image and sound move between pixels and apparent bodily realism while a second screen shows its artificial-agent data. The oscillation refuses a seamless resurrection: the more lifelike the surrogate becomes, the more visibly it remains alone, computational and detached from herd and habitat.
publics_text: Documented presentations include the 2019 Cooper Hewitt Design Triennial, FACT Liverpool in 2020, Onassis Stegi in 2021, *The Lost Rhino* at London’s Natural History Museum and the Natural History Museum Bern in 2022, and the 23rd Biennale of Sydney (**D/CR**). Encountered publics include museum, biennial, design, AI, natural-history and conservation audiences. The northern white rhino is represented through archival traces and simulation; living rhinos, rangers and habitat communities are not participants in the installation.
rq1: Extinction reaches many publics as a brief news event, while speculative de-extinction can make technological replacement appear more imaginable than long-term protection of living species, habitats and caretaking institutions.
rq2: The artwork uses life-size scale, charismatic animal presence, pixel-to-lifelike transformation, adaptive agent behaviour, archival herd footage, paired explanatory data and long-term institutional circulation.
rq3: A work criticising substitution must nevertheless make a compelling substitute. The isolated digital rhino can recentre AI laboratories, museums and technological virtuosity, while histories of hunting, conservation governance, colonial extraction, kinship and habitat are compressed into the absent background. Emotional encounter is documented only as an invitation; conservation action and changed priorities are not.
evaluation: A highly legible extinction critique with durable museum circulation, but no evidence that spectators change conservation priorities or action.
configuration: Brief public mourning and techno-resurrection optimism → deliberately unstable life-size surrogate → museum, AI and conservation publics → documented international circulation → substitution, charisma and institutional-authority tensions → keep the artificiality and missing habitat politically explicit.
evidence_boundary: Strong institutional evidence for commissioning, mechanism, collection status and exhibition trajectory; no audience or conservation-outcome evaluation. Sources: [artist project page](https://www.daisyginsberg.com/work/the-substitute) and [Biennale of Sydney collection record](https://artsandculture.google.com/asset/the-substitute-2019-alexandra-daisy-ginsberg/DwHfZFqUoU_yew).

medium: Performative multiuser multisensory VR; soft robotics; scent; food
occasions: IDFA DocLab premiere; Dutch Film Festival; Waag/Museumnacht and later bookings
publics: Ticketed immersive participants, festival observers, posthuman-design publics; organisms represented through hybrid roles
summary:
*Symbiosis* is a performative, multiuser and multisensory VR installation designed and produced by the Dutch collective Polymorf with Studio Biarritz and an extensive team of wearable, scent, food, performance and technical collaborators. It premiered at IDFA DocLab in 2021.

Participants choose speculative hybrid roles—among them human–animal, human–plant and human–technology bodies—then enter a shared post-Anthropocene world. Full-body movement, custom soft-robotic wearables, haptics, scent and role-specific vegetarian tastes extend the encounter beyond a headset. The individual stories converge in a collective eating ritual, making each visitor both performer and material condition for the others.
publics_text: The installation premiered at IDFA DocLab in 2021 and was later presented through the Dutch Film Festival, Polymorf’s studio, Waag/Museumnacht and further timed booking programmes (**D/CR**). It received IDFA’s Special Jury Award for Creative Technology (**D/CR**). Participating publics are small groups of booked immersive visitors supported by facilitators; observers, film/new-media and posthuman-design publics encounter the surrounding performance and documentation. Plants, animals, slime moulds and future entities are represented through designed hybrid roles rather than directly involved.
rq1: Posthuman interdependence is theoretically dense, and conventional VR isolates one viewer, privileges sight and leaves bodily relation outside the medium. The work also faces the challenge of making radical bodily difference inviting rather than punitive.
rq2: Tactics include role-based collective embodiment, theatrical facilitation, custom soft robotics, manipulated body schemas, haptics, scent, taste, food-sharing and a convergence from separate stories into a temporary public ritual.
rq3: Designed hybridity can collapse species specificity into pleasurable human fantasy. The future world largely replaces competition and conflict with symbiosis, stabilising a politically attractive harmony. Custom wearables, bodily handling, food, intensive staffing and timed ticketing also distribute access unevenly. Immersion may deepen affect for participants but does not demonstrate nonhuman benefit, ecological accuracy or durable action.
evaluation: A strong affective and relational artwork that expands VR beyond vision, while offering no evidence of nonhuman benefit or durable public action.
configuration: Abstract interdependence and visually isolated VR → multisensory hybrid embodiment plus collective food ritual → small ticketed participant publics and wider festival observers → documented performance circulation → fantasy, harmony, consent and access tensions → disclose speculation and evaluate interpretation beyond novelty.
evidence_boundary: Strong official and festival evidence for form, credits and presentations; no longitudinal public or ecological outcome evidence. Sources: [Polymorf project page](https://www.polymorf.nl/interaction/symbiosis/), [IDFA record](https://www.idfa.nl/en/cinema/bc2441ca-df8b-4d0d-9e2d-5c7085317fd0/symbiosis/) and [Waag presentation record](https://waag.org/en/article/becoming-other-experience-symbiosis-waag/).

title: Plant Radio
creators: Margrete Lodahl Rolighed, Ester Marie Aagaard, Marcus Due Jensen, Raune Frankjær, Lone Koefoed Hansen
occasions: Eight-home deployment; Maker Faire, Day Riverbed, Sustainable Spring Break; DIS 2022/2024
publics: Plant carers, household members, festival visitors, design researchers; plants instrumented
summary:
*Plant Radio* was developed from 2021–2022 onward by Margrete Lodahl Rolighed, Ester Marie Aagaard, Marcus Due Jensen, Raune Frankjær and Lone Koefoed Hansen. It is a portable device that translates plant electrical variation into sound, pulsing coloured light and a graph. In the supplied review image it is labelled **○11, [174]**, with photograph credit **© Margrete Lodahl Rolighed**; the reference number is local to that review.

Electrodes connect a plant to an EMG-like sensing circuit. The resulting variation is mapped through a portable radio-shaped device, allowing people to move it among houseplants, outdoor plants and other everyday settings. Crucially, the research compares brief public contact with a three-week domestic deployment, showing how interpretations change when the device enters routines of care, social negotiation and repeated uncertainty.
publics_text: The design was published as a DIS 2022 pictorial and studied across an eighteen-month programme reported at DIS 2024 (**D**). Public occasions included a local Maker Faire, Day Riverbed and Sustainable Spring Break. Eight self-identified plant lovers in five cities used it at home for three weeks, kept diaries, responded to twice-weekly prompts and joined a half-day workshop. Encountered publics included thousands of event attendees, but documented stops or conversations were far fewer. Plants, household members, event visitors and researchers formed different participating or affected publics.
rq1: Plant activity is imperceptible, plants readily recede into domestic background, and brief public encounters rarely sustain a new relation. Plant care can also be socially awkward or reduced to optimisation.
rq2: Tactics include ambiguous sonification, light and graph; portability; repeated home cohabitation; diaries and open prompts; a reflective workshop; and researcher-supported conversations at public events.
rq3: The sensor mediates electrical variation; it does not reveal plant speech, emotion or intention. Ambiguity enabled curiosity but also guilt and anthropomorphic projection. The eight home participants were already plant lovers, public-event data were opportunistic, and the study did not establish lasting behaviour, plant welfare or ecological action.
evaluation: One of the strongest additions because it compares domestic duration with public brevity and exposes its own epistemic limits.
configuration: Imperceptible plant activity and shallow event time → portable ambiguous sensing plus domestic duration → plant-loving households and mixed festival publics → rich small-sample interpretation evidence → mediation, stigma, projection and generalisability tensions → strongest as a comparison of duration and context, not proof of ecological transformation.
evidence_boundary: Strong, peer-reviewed qualitative evidence for eight home deployments and multiple public encounters; no nonhuman-outcome or longitudinal post-study evidence. Ikeya, Barati and Wensveen's 2025 review confirms the supplied visual label **○11**, bibliography number **[174]**, and credit **© Margrete Lodahl Rolighed**. Sources: [project page](https://www.marcusduejensen.com/plantradio.html), [DIS 2022 DOI](https://doi.org/10.1145/3532106.3533517), [DIS 2024 DOI](https://doi.org/10.1145/3643834.3661586), [`references/ikeya2025aesthetics.md`](../ikeya2025aesthetics.md) and [`research/.../mthd-0038...md`](../../research/more-than-human-design-review/knowledge/papers/mthd-0038-2024-encountering-human-plant-relations-a-discussion-of-how-interaction-design-can-encourage-human-sensib.md).
format: portable plant-electrical sonification device

csv.rq3: Sensing is mediation rather than plant speech; visible plant care can be socially stigmatised and no ecological outcome is established.

title: Plant Sensorium
creators: Margrete Lodahl Rolighed, Marcus Due Jensen, Martin Rossing Mørk, Lone Koefoed Hansen and collaborators
entity: Twelve potted plants and touch relations
occasions: Maker Faire, Processing Day, SEEK festival
publics: Festival visitors, families/makers, artists/researchers; plants touched/instrumented
summary:
*Plant Sensorium* was developed in 2022–2023 by Margrete Lodahl Rolighed, Marcus Due Jensen, Martin Rossing Mørk and Lone Koefoed Hansen. It is a walk-in installation of twelve potted plants equipped with capacitive touch sensing, distinct sounds and LED responses.

Visitors move among plants and touch leaves or stems. Touch triggers sonic and luminous events, enabling individual and collective composition. Wind, insects and accidental contact may also enter the event. The semi-confined arrangement and a researcher available for conversation turn the installation into a public contact zone rather than a solitary dashboard.
publics_text: The installation was adapted across Maker Faire, Processing Day and SEEK public events and analysed in the 2024 DIS paper on human–plant encounters (**D**). Event visitors typically spent approximately one to ten minutes. Participating publics included researchers, facilitators and visitors who touched or composed together. The plants were living participants materially installed in the interaction; event organisers and plant carers were responsible for their conditions.
rq1: Plant relations need a low-threshold public form beyond specialist plant science and posthuman theory. At the same time, event attention is brief and socially shaped.
rq2: Tactics include bodily touch, immediate sound/light response, collective composition, a spatially legible plant arrangement, festival placement, conversational facilitation and adaptive restaging.
rq3: Capacitive sensors primarily detect contact; they do not establish plant intention. The staging may therefore imply that plants deliberately respond to visitors. Touch can generate intimacy but also normalise human access to plant bodies. Short encounters and unknown event denominators make durable interpretation difficult to evaluate.
evaluation: A good reach and co-composition case, but epistemically weaker than Plant Radio.
configuration: Backgrounded plants and specialist discourse → touch-triggered public co-composition → maker, art and festival publics → repeated event encounters → staged-agency, bodily-access and brevity tensions → disclose what the sensor detects and compare immediate delight with longer relations.
evidence_boundary: Strong design and multi-event documentation; thinner audience data than the related home deployment and no established plant/ecological outcome. Sources: [project page](https://www.marcusduejensen.com/plant-sensorium.html), [DIS 2024 DOI](https://doi.org/10.1145/3643834.3661586) and [`research/.../mthd-0038...md`](../../research/more-than-human-design-review/knowledge/papers/mthd-0038-2024-encountering-human-plant-relations-a-discussion-of-how-interaction-design-can-encourage-human-sensib.md).
format: walk-in touch-triggered sound/light installation

csv.rq2: Bodily touch, collective sound composition, LEDs, festival placement and adaptive restaging.
csv.rq3: Capacitive sensors detect human touch rather than plant intention; the staging may imply responsive agency that the plants do not exercise.

title: Plant Disco
creators: Margrete Lodahl Rolighed, Lone Koefoed Hansen
entity: Soil biota, roots, fungi and worms
occasions: Aarhus design demonstration/exhibition; DRS 2026
publics: Exhibition visitors, design researchers; soil communities and added worms affected
summary:
*Plant Disco* is a 2025–2026 design-research project by Margrete Lodahl Rolighed and Lone Koefoed Hansen. It listens to soil through a contact microphone and maps detected vibration to headphones and the movement or light of a mirror ball.

The work asks visitors to put an ear to soil life whose activity may be faint, intermittent or absent during exhibition time. Silence, latency and uncertainty are not merely failures but part of the encounter. Yet the design process also records a revealing intervention: twenty-four earthworms were added to help ensure audible activity, exposing pressure to make nonhuman life perform on demand.
publics_text: The work developed through Aarhus-based design and exhibition activity and is documented in a DRS 2026 research paper (**D**). Participating publics include the designers, exhibition organisers and visitors using the headphones. Soil, roots, fungi, microorganisms and added worms are living or material participants. The work is still an early critical prototype rather than a repeatedly evaluated public programme.
rq1: Soil life is spatially concealed and follows rhythms incompatible with gallery expectations for immediate feedback. Silence risks being read as malfunction rather than as an ecological condition.
rq2: Tactics include contact-microphone ecoacoustics, intimate headphone listening, vibration-driven light/motion, humour, silence and temporal friction.
rq3: Adding worms to guarantee audibility is the project’s central political disclosure: sensitisation can instrumentalise the life it celebrates. The mirror ball makes soil activity culturally playful but may reward constant output. The design’s strength lies in exposing, not resolving, the conflict between exhibition time and organismal time.
evaluation: A particularly strong RQ3 reflexive case, but not a success model or long-tested public work.
configuration: Hidden and intermittent soil activity → intimate amplified listening plus deliberately visible latency → design/exhibition public → early encounter evidence → instrumentalisation and performance-demand tensions → retain as a reflexive RQ3 case rather than a success model.
evidence_boundary: Peer-reviewed documentation supports the design process and twenty-four-worm episode; audience and organismal consequences remain thin. Sources: [DRS 2026 paper record](https://dl.designresearchsociety.org/drs-conference-papers/drs2026/researchpapers/484) and [`research/.../mthd-0090...md`](../../research/more-than-human-design-review/knowledge/papers/mthd-0090-2026-putting-an-ear-to-the-ground-attending-to-frictions-in-human-machine-soil-temporalities.md).

title: The More-than-Human Talking Stick
creators: Margrete Lodahl Rolighed, Morten Bech Laugesen, Eva Eriksson, Lone Koefoed Hansen
occasions: Permaculture community fieldwork; CHI EA 2026
publics: Garden-community participants, meeting participants, HCI researchers; nonhumans represented
summary:
*The More-than-Human Talking Stick* is a 2026 CHI Extended Abstracts project by Margrete Lodahl Rolighed, Morten Bech Laugesen, Eva Eriksson and Lone Koefoed Hansen. It emerged from fieldwork in a permaculture garden community.

The researchers derived three principles—consideration, connectedness and dynamics—and used them to create an artefact that intervenes with a more-than-human voice during mostly-human conversations. The familiar talking-stick form moves the problem from sensing an organism to governing discussion: when and how should relations with soil, plants, weather and other beings interrupt a human meeting?
publics_text: The situated field context was a permaculture garden community, and the documented public occasion is CHI 2026 scholarly dissemination (**D**). Garden participants and researchers form the participating public; CHI readers and attendees are the encountered public. Garden organisms and processes are represented through the artefact. The relevant future decision-capable publics would be garden groups, planners or organisations deliberating about place, but changed decisions have not been demonstrated.
rq1: Meetings about ecological places remain linguistically and procedurally human. More-than-human agencies can disappear even when participants endorse ecological values.
rq2: Tactics include situated fieldwork, three process principles, a culturally recognisable turn-taking object and an interruption that inserts a more-than-human proxy voice.
rq3: Any inserted voice is authored and selective. Whoever writes the interruption gains procedural authority to decide what the garden says and when humans must listen. An extended abstract supplies too little evidence to know who accepts the proxy, whether disagreement is possible or whether decisions change.
evaluation: A useful governance prototype for RQ3, presently watchlist due to thin empirical reporting.
configuration: Mostly-human ecological deliberation → field-derived proxy intervention in turn-taking → garden and HCI publics → prototype and conceptual evidence → representation and procedural-authority tensions → retain on watchlist pending meeting-level and decision-level study.
evidence_boundary: Peer-reviewed but brief; no robust evaluation or decision outcome. Sources: [Aarhus University record](https://pure.au.dk/portal/en/publications/the-more-than-human-talking-stick-design-principles-for-multispec/) and [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1145/3772363.3798517).
format: situated conversational artifact

csv.rq1: Mostly-human meetings exclude more-than-human agencies even when discussing ecological places.
csv.rq2: Fieldwork-derived principles of consideration, connectedness and dynamics; an artifact interrupts conversation with a more-than-human voice.
csv.rq3: Any such voice is authored and selective; an extended abstract offers little evidence about who accepts the proxy or how decisions change.

title: Slime-mould-integrated smartwatch
creators: Jasmine Lu, Pedro Lopes
occasions: Five-person 9–14-day study; UIST 2022
publics: Study participants, HCI/device publics; slime mould maintained and neglected
summary:
This 2022 UIST study by Jasmine Lu and Pedro Lopes integrates the slime mould *Physarum polycephalum* into a functioning smartwatch. The organism forms a conductive living wire required for the watch’s heart-rate sensing function.

Users must feed and maintain the slime mould for the device to operate. Five participants wore the watch for nine to fourteen days: they first cared for it, then followed researcher instructions to neglect it, allowing desiccation and later revival to become perceptible. The device makes maintenance and interdependence materially unavoidable rather than presenting them as an informational message.
publics_text: The principal public occasion was the UIST 2022 paper and demonstration/research circulation (**D**). Five wearers and the researchers were participating publics; HCI, wearable and biodesign audiences were encountered publics. *Physarum* was a living functional participant. Device manufacturers and research-ethics communities are potential decision-capable publics, though no adoption was studied.
rq1: Electronics usually conceal maintenance relations and present reliable function as independent of living conditions. Microbial or protist life is especially easy to treat as interchangeable material.
rq2: Tactics include functional dependency, daily care, visible growth/desiccation, embodied wearing, a nine-to-fourteen-day deployment and the possibility of revival.
rq3: The slime mould remains a component enlisted for human sensing. Researcher-prescribed neglect makes the ethical tension experimentally legible but also deliberately withholds care. Participants’ responsibility and attachment are evidence about human interpretation, not organismal consent, reciprocity or welfare.
evaluation: A rare evaluated care interaction and essential critical living-media case.
configuration: Hidden device maintenance and living materiality → care-dependent functional circuit → five wearers and HCI/biodesign public → unusually concrete longitudinal interaction evidence → componentisation, prescribed-neglect and human-proxy tensions → treat care claims separately from nonhuman benefit.
evidence_boundary: Strong peer-reviewed evidence for the prototype and five participant experiences; weak generalisability and no direct nonhuman-outcome measure. Sources: [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1145/3526113.3545629) and [`references/lu2022integrating.md`](../lu2022integrating.md).
format: living-organism wearable device

csv.rq1: Device users rarely notice maintenance, interdependence or the life conditions hidden inside electronics.
csv.rq2: A living conductive wire enables heart-rate sensing only when cared for; nine-to-fourteen-day wear study makes neglect and revival tangible.
csv.rq3: The slime mould is still a functional component, and researchers prescribed neglect; human attachment is not organismal consent, reciprocity or welfare.

title: Designing Plant-Driven Actuators for Robots to Grow, Age, and Decay
creators: Yuhan Hu, Jasmine Lu and four collaborators
occasions: DIS 2024
publics: HCI/robotics/design publics; plants incorporated into prototypes
summary:
This 2024 DIS project is by Yuhan Hu, Jasmine Lu, Nathan Scinto-Madonich, Miguel Alfonso Pineros, Pedro Lopes and Guy Hoffman. Yuhan Hu is distinct from Youyang Hu, whose works appear in W29–W32.

The authors develop plant–robot prototypes in which biological growth and change become actuation. Rather than demanding immediate, repeatable mechanical motion, the project treats growth, ageing and decay as processes that can transform a robotic artefact over time. Its main contribution is a design space for plant-driven actuation and hybrid robot temporalities.
publics_text: The primary presentation was the DIS 2024 conference and proceedings (**D**). Researchers and prototype builders were participating publics; interaction-design, robotics and biodesign communities were encountered publics. Living plants were functional material participants. No broad gallery audience or long-term deployment public was reported.
rq1: Robotics privileges speed, repeatability, control and durability. Those norms exclude biological time and hide the maintenance or death involved in hybrid systems.
rq2: Tactics include using plant growth as actuation, designing for slow transformation, accepting ageing and decay and offering a comparative grammar for plant–robot relationships.
rq3: Plants may become components whose unpredictability is aesthetically or mechanically mined. Designers still select species, constrain growth and define successful motion. Short prototypes cannot show long-term plant health, reciprocal benefit, disposal or public interpretation.
evaluation: A valuable decay and temporality comparator, but evidence is currently stronger for mechanism than relation.
configuration: Mechanistic robotic time → plant growth and decay as actuation → DIS/robotics/biodesign publics → prototype-level mechanism evidence → componentisation, care and lifecycle tensions → use as a temporality comparator, not a demonstrated relational outcome.
evidence_boundary: Peer-reviewed and strong for the design space; limited for duration, plant consequences and publics. Sources: [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1145/3643834.3661519) and [Jasmine Lu’s publication list](https://jasminelu.site/Publications).
format: plant-robot actuator prototypes

csv.rq2: Plant growth as actuation, slow transformation, ageing, decay and a design-space grammar for hybrid robots.

title: Cat Royale
creators: Blast Theory with university and animal-welfare collaborators
entity: Three domestic cats and autonomous systems
medium: Species-informed enclosure; robot play; public film
occasions: World Science Festival Brisbane; Science Gallery London; touring/online film
publics: Cats/owner, welfare experts, artists/operators, festival/gallery and AI publics
summary:
*Cat Royale* (2023) was made by Blast Theory with the University of Nottingham’s Mixed Reality Lab, Open University and University of Lincoln collaborators, feline-welfare expertise and RSPCA involvement. The live participants were three related cats—Ghostbuster, Pumpkin and Clover—and a semi-autonomous robot arm.

The cats occupied a purpose-built “cat utopia” for two three-hour sessions per day across twelve days. The system proposed toy or treat activities; a human artist approved or rejected them and an operator could intervene or stop the robot. More than five hundred activities were offered. An independent welfare officer used a stress scale every fifteen minutes, while engagement in play was rated separately. Eight cameras supported delayed public streaming and later film installations.
publics_text: The world premiere was presented as a delayed stream at World Science Festival Brisbane/Curiocity from 22 March to 2 April 2023, including Queen Street Mall. A seven-hour film appeared in *AI: Who’s Looking After Me?* at Science Gallery London from 21 June 2023 to 20 January 2024, with further presentation at Wales Millennium Centre (**D/CR**). Blast Theory reports an audience above 400,000 for Brisbane; this is creator-reported exposure, not verified engagement. Cats, owner, operators, welfare officer, scientists and artists were participating publics; festival, online and gallery viewers were encountered publics.
rq1: AI-mediated animal care is expanding but its operation, labour and welfare assumptions are difficult for non-specialists to inspect. Public debate often oscillates between novelty and fear.
rq2: Tactics include a species-informed enclosure, dens and elevated retreats, tangible capturable toys, mixed-initiative robot control, separate stress and play measures, continuous welfare oversight, daily highlight storytelling and explicit public ambiguity about AI care.
rq3: Cats could retreat from the robot but not freely determine the overall research/exhibition situation; they spent time outside the enclosure each day under human management. Engagement is not welfare, and happiness remained a proxy rather than a demonstrated internal state. Human approval, safety intervention, repair and cleaning were indispensable to apparent autonomy. Three cats over twelve days cannot establish general home suitability or durable benefit.
evaluation: The strongest new bridge-spanning case because it combines public reach with documented welfare governance and unresolved consent.
configuration: Opaque AI–animal care → publicly visible whole-world experiment with welfare governance → cats, expert teams and large festival/gallery publics → unusually rich process evidence, no formal welfare or audience-effect analysis → consent, proxy, spectacle and invisible-labour tensions → strongest bridge-spanning case when presented with its unresolved limits.
evidence_boundary: Strong primary and peer-reviewed process evidence; the CHI paper explicitly does not formally evaluate happiness, play effectiveness or public reception. Sources: [Blast Theory project page](https://www.blasttheory.co.uk/projects/cat-royale/), [CHI 2024 DOI](https://doi.org/10.1145/3613904.3642115) and [`research/.../mthd-0186...md`](../../research/more-than-human-design-review/knowledge/papers/mthd-0186-2024-designing-multispecies-worlds-for-robots-cats-and-humans.md).

title: We Live in an Ocean of Air
creators: Marshmallow Laser Feast and collaborators
entity: Giant sequoia, breath and forest metabolism
occasions: London immersive run; ArtScience Museum Singapore 2022; ACMI 2023–2024; later editions
publics: Ticketed immersive/museum visitors, climate and forest publics
summary:
*We Live in an Ocean of Air* is a multisensory immersive work by Marshmallow Laser Feast, first presented in virtual reality in 2018 and subsequently adapted as VR and video editions through 2023 and beyond. It draws on a 2016 LiDAR scan and ecological survey in Sequoia National Park.

Breath sensing and real-time graphics place the visitor inside flows linking lungs, blood, leaves, phloem, mycelium and atmosphere. The giant sequoia and forest are rendered at scales inaccessible to unaided perception. Breath becomes an embodied interface through which plant–animal gas exchange is felt as immediate interdependence.
publics_text: Documented presentations include Saatchi Gallery, London (7 December 2018–5 May 2019); PHI Centre, Montréal (29 September 2021–16 January 2022); ArtScience Museum, Singapore (28 May–2 October 2022); and the video edition within *Works of Nature* at ACMI, Melbourne (23 November 2023–14 April 2024), among other venues (**D**). Encountered publics are primarily ticketed museum, gallery, tourist and immersive-media audiences. Artists, scientists, technicians and venue staff are participating publics; the sequoia forest is scanned and represented rather than live.
rq1: Plant–human gas exchange is invisible and climate interdependence is abstract. Facts and statistics may not create a bodily sense of dependence.
rq2: Tactics include breath sensing, real-time visualisation, LiDAR forest data, enormous shifts of scale, spatial sound, guided immersion and multiple editions suited to international touring.
rq3: Human breath remains the privileged entry point, and reciprocity may be simplified into a harmonious closed loop. Scientific data becomes a high-production immersive spectacle, with ticketing and technical infrastructure shaping access. Exhibition history demonstrates circulation, not ecological action.
evaluation: A highly effective affective bridge with substantial circulation, but no demonstrated ecological action.
configuration: Invisible atmospheric interdependence → breath-coupled forest immersion → international museum and VR publics → strong touring evidence → human-entry, harmony, access and spectacle tensions → pair affective reciprocity with situated forest politics and measurable next steps.
evidence_boundary: Excellent official exhibition record and clear technical-artistic framing; no evidence that the work caused lasting environmental behaviour or policy. Sources: [official project page](https://marshmallowlaserfeast.com/project/we-live-in-an-ocean-of-air/) and [*Works of Nature* archive](https://marshmallowlaserfeast.com/project/works-of-nature/).

format: multisensory VR/video installation

title: Treehugger: Wawona
creators: Marshmallow Laser Feast and collaborators
medium: Tree sculpture; VR; touch; scent; audio
occasions: Cinekid/STRP/Southbank commissions; Tribeca 2017; later touring
publics: Festival/family and immersive-art publics; redwood/forest relations represented
summary:
*Treehugger: Wawona* is a 2016–2017 interactive installation by Marshmallow Laser Feast, created by Barney Steel, Robin McNicholas and Ersin Han Ersin with collaborators in sound, scent and production. It centres on a sculptural giant-redwood portal and a seven-minute VR experience.

A visitor embraces or leans into the physical tree form, places their head into a knot-like opening and enters a virtual sequoia. Visualised xylem and internal flows, binaural sound, touch and scent invite movement from external monumentality into “tree time.” The longer embrace promises a deeper perceptual entry into processes beyond ordinary human scale.
publics_text: The work was commissioned by Cinekid Foundation, STRP, Southbank Centre and Migrations. Presentations included Cinekid MediaLab (2016), Southbank Centre Winter Festival (December 2016), STRP Biennial in Eindhoven (2017), Migrations in Wales and Tribeca Film Festival’s Storyscapes programme in 2017 (**D**). Encountered publics included families, children, festival visitors, immersive-media and art audiences. Production teams and venue facilitators were participating publics. The redwood is a simulated and sculptural subject, not a live participant.
rq1: Tree physiology and millennial tree time exceed ordinary human perception. Giant sequoias are also geographically inaccessible to most festival publics.
rq2: Tactics include physical embrace, a head-in-tree portal, VR, haptic contact, scent, binaural audio, internal-scale visualisation, a short memorable narrative and family-oriented festival circulation.
rq3: The tree becomes an interface and spectacular avatar. Simulated intimacy may suggest that technological access equals knowing a tree, while actual forest territories, fire histories, conservation and Indigenous relations remain offstage. The seven-minute format expands reach but compresses tree time into an attraction.
evaluation: An influential, memorable reach case; include beside slower and less spectacular plant practices to expose spectacle bias.
configuration: Inaccessible physiology and deep time → multisensory bodily portal → family/festival/immersive publics → strong touring and award visibility → avatar, simulation and spectacle-bias tensions → compare with slower living-plant practices and restore place-specific forest context.
evidence_boundary: Strong commissioning and festival documentation; no audience study or conservation-outcome evidence. Sources: [Tribeca Festival archive](https://tribecafilm.com/festival/archive/treehugger-wawona-2017) and [STRP Biennial archive](https://strp.nl/nl/evenementen/biennial-2017-senses-sensors).

title: terra0 / self-owning forest
creators: terra0 collective
medium: White paper; blockchain and institutional experiments
occasions: Carnegie International, Venice Architecture Biennale, CCA, The Shed and other venues
publics: Art/architecture, blockchain, legal/economic and environmental publics; forests represented/implicated
summary:
*terra0* is a collective and ongoing art–research programme initiated in 2016. Its foundational “self-owning forest” proposal imagines a forest using sensors, computation and blockchain smart contracts to administer resources, accumulate capital and eventually purchase or extend control over itself.

The proposal relocates more-than-human agency from sensory empathy to legal and economic infrastructure. In the canonical scenario, a forest evaluates resources and sells logging licences through smart contracts until it can repay initial human owners and become economically self-possessing. Subsequent works and exhibitions have explored automated governance, ownership and value rather than establishing a literally autonomous forest.
publics_text: The project has circulated since the May 2016 white paper through art, architecture, design, blockchain and research exhibitions, publications and talks (**D; individual installation history should be cited per version**). Participating publics include collective members, programmers, curators and institutional partners. Encountered publics include art, architecture, legal-technology and crypto communities. Forests are modelled as legal-economic actors. Legislatures, courts, landowners and financial institutions are the actual decision-capable publics, but none transferred full self-ownership to a forest in the documented foundational case.
rq1: Forests lack standing and economic agency inside the institutions that govern extraction, land title and investment. Sensory awareness alone does not change those structures.
rq2: Tactics include speculative legal design, smart contracts, autonomous-agent rhetoric, sensor-based resource accounting, revenue cycles and institutional reframing of ownership.
rq3: The forest must enter a market and may sell timber in order to purchase autonomy, reproducing the extractive logic being criticised. Programmers define the rules, humans own infrastructure and law decides whether the entity exists. “Self-owning” is therefore a productive contradiction and political proposition, not a verified legal fact.
evaluation: An indispensable governance comparator, best used as a productive contradiction rather than a realised autonomous forest.
configuration: Institutional absence of forest agency → speculative code/legal-economic personhood → art, architecture, blockchain and governance publics → sustained conceptual circulation, unrealised literal autonomy → market-dependence, code-authorship and jurisdiction tensions → use as a governance comparator and state implementation status precisely.
evidence_boundary: Strong for the 2016 concept and subsequent artistic discourse; no evidence of a forest achieving literal legal self-ownership. Sources: [terra0 official archive](https://terra0.org/) and [2016 white paper](https://terra0.org/assets/pdf/terra0_white_paper_2016.pdf).
format: blockchain governance concept and experiments

csv.rq1: Forests lack legal/economic agency within institutions that determine extraction and ownership.
csv.rq2: Smart contracts, self-ownership speculation, revenue cycles and institutional/legal reframing.
csv.rq3: The forest must enter the market and potentially sell timber to buy autonomy; code authors and legal systems still define its agency.

title: Project Habitate
creators: Yuning Chen, Yishan Qin, Tom Hartley with scientific collaborators
occasions: Dutch Design Week 2020; ST+ARTS/CyberArts 2021 circulation
publics: Design/festival publics, wearers as proposed conservation participants, lichen and ash ecologies affected
summary:
*Project Habitate* is a 2020 biomimetic wearable by Yuning Chen, Yishan Qin and Tom Hartley, developed with lichen, ecology, engineering and material collaborators. It responds to lichens threatened by secondary extinction following the decline of ash trees in temperate Europe.

The team studied properties of ash bark—including texture, light permeability, porosity and pH—and developed a wearable substrate proposed to sustain overlooked lichen species during the ecological gap created by host-tree loss. Human movement is enlisted to disperse lichen spores outdoors. The work reverses the usual grammar of “ecosystem services”: instead of asking what nonhumans do for people, it asks people to become temporary habitat and perform ecological labour.
publics_text: Public circulation included Dutch Design Week in 2020 and recognition/exhibition through the 2021 ST+ARTS/CyberArts context, including presentation associated with the ST+ARTS Festival at BOZAR in Brussels (**D/CR**). Encountered publics include design-festival, biomimicry, conservation and innovation audiences. Wearers are imagined as participating conservation publics. Lichens and ash-tree ecologies are intended beneficiaries and materially affected publics if the proposal is deployed. Ecologists, conservation organisations, land managers and biosecurity authorities are the relevant decision-capable publics.
rq1: Lichen reproduction and secondary extinction are slow, small-scale and publicly overshadowed by the loss of the more charismatic host tree. Conventional ecosystem-service language also makes nonhuman value legible mainly through benefit to humans.
rq2: Tactics include ash-bark biomimicry, a body-worn habitat, tactile material demonstration, human mobility as spore-dispersal infrastructure and an activist reversal of ecosystem-service roles.
rq3: Reversing service does not eliminate human control: people choose the lichen, fabricate its substrate and determine where it moves. Public project pages do not provide survival rates, successful attachment, ecological fit, unintended dispersal or long-term habitat outcomes. The wearable may therefore perform conservation symbolically while creating untested ecological obligations.
evaluation: A concrete action proposition and useful conservation comparator, but not evidence of successful lichen restoration.
configuration: Overlooked secondary extinction and asymmetrical service language → wearable habitat and mobile spore proposition → design/festival and prospective conservation publics → documented prototype and circulation, unverified ecological function → stewardship, ecological-fit and biosecurity tensions → describe as participatory-conservation proposition, not achieved restoration.
evidence_boundary: Strong for creators, concept and public circulation; absent peer-reviewed ecological validation or conservation outcome. Sources: [Yuning Chen project archive](https://alienyuning.net/projects), [RCA/Imperial alumni project account](https://www.alienyuning.com/about-) and [`research/five_practitioner_rq_annotation_review_2026-08-29.md`](../../research/five_practitioner_rq_annotation_review_2026-08-29.md).
format: biomimetic wearable habitat and participatory-conservation proposition

csv.rq1: Lichen secondary extinction, host loss and slow reproduction are difficult to notice, while ecosystem-service language normally assigns service only to nonhumans.
csv.rq2: Ash-bark biomimicry, wearable habitat, human mobility and proposed spore dispersal reverse ecosystem-service roles.
csv.rq3: Humans still design and move the habitat; survival, ecological fit, dispersal risk and actual conservation effect are not publicly validated.

title: Plant Reality Set
creators: Yuning Chen, Lamp Lee, Naomi Nakayama
entity: Plant light, wind and root-water perception
occasions: Royal College of Art 2021 graduate showcase; design-award/exhibition circulation
publics: Graduate-show/design publics, wearable participants; plants represented through scientific analogy
summary:
*Plant Reality Set* is a 2021 graduate project by Yuning Chen with Lamp Lee and Naomi Nakayama. It comprises three wearable sensory interfaces—*Touch Symphony*, *The Taste of Light* and *Root Acoustic*—designed around plant relations with wind, light and underground water.

Participants taste mapped differences in light spectra, feel electrical stimulation associated with wind-related signals and listen to water acoustics framed through root sensing. The project explicitly distinguishes “meaningful analogy” from phenomenological translation. Light becomes taste because both light for plants and food for humans function as energy, not because the designer claims humans literally feel photosynthesis.
publics_text: The primary documented public occasion was the Royal College of Art’s 2021 graduate showcase, with subsequent visibility through design-award and exhibition circuits listed in Chen’s practice record (**D/CR; version-to-venue mapping is incomplete**). Encountered publics include graduate-show visitors, designers, biomimicry and sensory-interface audiences. Wearers are participating publics. Plants are represented through botanical research and analogy rather than sensed as live co-performers. Botanists and access/disability communities are interpretively relevant, but their direct participation is not documented.
rq1: Plant responses to light, wind and root-zone water exceed ordinary human perception. Visual dominance and the phrase “plant perspective” can falsely suggest transparent access to plant life.
rq2: Tactics include cross-modal sensory substitution, taste, skin stimulation, sound, bodily wearables and an explicit analogy principle that acknowledges difference.
rq3: Declaring analogy is an important epistemic safeguard but does not remove translation authority. Designers decide why light becomes taste, which spectra matter and how variable plant species are compressed into a general wearable “plant reality.” Electrical and oral interfaces also distribute accessibility, comfort and consent unevenly among human participants.
evaluation: An important epistemic-humility comparator with strong sensory invitation and limited public/outcome evidence.
configuration: Inaccessible plant sensing and visual dominance → explicit cross-modal analogy through wearables → graduate/design and embodied participant publics → documented artefact and showcase → mapping-authority, species-generalisation and accessibility tensions → publish the mapping chain and avoid claims of perceptual equivalence.
evidence_boundary: Strong official description and RCA presentation evidence; no formal audience study, plant validation or behavioural/ecological outcome. Sources: [RCA 2021 project page](https://2021.rca.ac.uk/students/yuning-chan/), [Yuning Chen project archive](https://alienyuning.net/projects) and [`research/five_practitioner_rq_annotation_review_2026-08-29.md`](../../research/five_practitioner_rq_annotation_review_2026-08-29.md).
