title: Microbial Revolt
creators: Yuning Chen, Larissa Pschetz
entity: Laboratory microbes, tools and waste ecologies
occasions: Three workshops over two months; CHI 2024, Honolulu; related bioart circulation
publics: 28 workshop participants, 16 interviewees, biodesign/biology/HCI publics, regulators; microbes represented
summary:
*Microbial Revolt* is a 2023–2024 participatory design intervention and artefact-making project by Yuning Chen and Larissa Pschetz. Across three workshops, biologists and designers reinterpreted laboratory breakdown and redesigned tools through the speculative possibility of microbial nonparticipation, producing 24 named Microbial Chindogu artefacts.

Participants first compare the life of an organism in feral and laboratory settings. They then temporarily read death, low growth, escape, resistance or contamination through a “revolt” lens and create Microbial Chindogu: tools deliberately useless for humans but potentially supportive of microbial refusal or escape. Follow-up interviews extend the provocation into proposals concerning alternative sterilisation, mixed cultures, traffic maps, liminal design-biolabs, documentation and regulator collaboration.
publics_text: Three one-to-two-hour workshops were held over two months—two face-to-face and one online—with 28 designers and biologists (**D**). Sixteen journal responses and 24 Chindogu inventions were analysed, and 16 follow-up interviews were conducted, five with workshop participants and eleven with additional practitioners. The work was published and presented at CHI 2024 in Honolulu and circulated through bioart contexts, including BAD Award selection (**D**). Microbes, strains, wild samples, tools, waste ecologies and regulators form affected or decision-capable publics, although microbial perspectives are necessarily proxied.
rq1: Microbial scale and laboratory conventions hide organismal time, labour, death, escape and ecological origin. Protocols classify anomalous outcomes as human error or contamination and provide no established channel for nonparticipation.
rq2: Tactics include feral/lab comparison, provocative role reframing, Chindogu making, balanced disciplinary discussion, follow-up interviews and translation from speculative objection into biosafety and infrastructure proposals.
rq3: “Revolt” grants political visibility but remains an anthropomorphic thinking tool, not evidence of microbial intention. Adversarial language can cast microbes as threats, while openness, intimacy, mixed cultures and wild sampling can create genuine environmental and health risks. Standardised laboratory control and design-studio freedom are not simple bad/good opposites; they allocate different responsibilities.
evaluation: One of the strongest complete RQ1-RQ3 cases because provocation develops into accountable infrastructure proposals.
configuration: Hidden microbial labour and protocol-defined error → revolt provocation plus counter-useful toolmaking → biologist, designer, bioart and HCI publics → substantial workshop/interview evidence → anthropomorphism, safety and governance tensions → preserve revolt as a heuristic and pursue validated, accountable infrastructure changes.
evidence_boundary: One of the portfolio’s strongest peer-reviewed participatory-design cases: 28 workshop participants, 24 artefacts and 16 interviews. The portfolio unit is the intervention and its realised artefacts, not the CHI paper or workshop procedure alone. Proposed sterilisation, mixed-culture and governance adaptations were not technically validated, and no microbial preference or welfare was established. Sources: [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1145/3613904.3641981), [`references/chen2024microbial.md`](../chen2024microbial.md) and [`research/.../mthd-0040...md`](../../research/more-than-human-design-review/knowledge/papers/mthd-0040-2024-microbial-revolt-redefining-biolab-tools-and-practices-for-more-than-human-care-ecologies.md).

format: three workshops, Microbial Chindogu and follow-up interviews

csv.rq3: Revolt is an anthropomorphic thinking tool, not microbial-intention evidence; openness, mixed cultures and wild sampling also create biosafety and environmental risks.

title: Manifesting the Spirits of Asilomar
creators: Josh Evans, Erika Szymanski, Tarsh Bates, Devon Ward, Yuning Chen
entity: Laboratory organisms, conference place and hidden sustainers of biotechnology
occasions: The Spirit of Asilomar and the Future of Biotechnology, Asilomar Conference Grounds, February 2025
publics: Biotechnology, history/STS and policy-facing conference publics; laboratory organisms, staff and place histories represented
summary:
*Manifesting the Spirits of Asilomar* comprises two artistic interventions created for *The Spirit of Asilomar and the Future of Biotechnology* conference in February 2025. *Bevergising the Spirits of Asilomar* is credited to Josh Evans and Erika Szymanski, with visual design by Evans, Szymanski and Yuning Chen. *Scents of Asilomar* is credited to Tarsh Bates, Devon Ward and Yuning Chen. They are treated as one situated project because both materialise marginalised “spirits” of the same conference history.

One intervention turns the metaphorical spirits of Asilomar into literal beverages served during the conference cocktail hour. The other gathers scents carrying fragments of local and biotechnology histories and stages a collective distillation. Together they make place, laboratory organisms, women staff, maintenance and other backgrounded contributors sensorially present inside a gathering explicitly revisiting the governance legacy of recombinant DNA.
publics_text: The works were presented at the Asilomar Hotel & Conference Grounds during the 2025 Gordon Cain Conference, organised by Rice University, Stanford University and the Science History Institute (**D/CR**). The event convened historians, scientists and other biotechnology-facing experts to debate AI, pathogen research, biological weapons, containment, bioeconomy and flourishing, with art and culture built into the programme (**D**). Conference delegates were participating and decision-capable publics; wider public access was bounded, although the conference included an evening public lecture. Laboratory organisms, historical staff and the site were represented through the artists’ selected stories and materials.
rq1: Canonical accounts of biotechnology governance foreground named scientists, formal declarations and abstract risks. They background the organisms that bore experimental risk, the places and care infrastructures sustaining debate, and marginalised human labour.
rq2: The works use literalised wordplay, beverage service, scent, collective distillation, situated storytelling and insertion into the conference’s own hospitality ritual. Rather than address a generic gallery public, they intervene where biotechnology history and future governance are actively discussed.
rq3: Reaching a small decision-capable public can be more consequential than maximising footfall, but the invitation-bounded setting also reproduces elite access. Makers and hosts decide which histories become drinkable or smellable, and sensory participation raises consent, allergy, safety and cultural-translation questions. Organisms and overlooked workers gain symbolic presence without authority to correct the representation or evidence that institutions redistributed power afterward.
evaluation: A sharply situated art intervention that reaches biotechnology decision publics, with limited documentation of reception or institutional consequence.
configuration: Elite, human-centred biotechnology memory → drinks, scents and collective distillation inside the commemorative conference → expert and policy-facing public → documented situated presentation → proxy, access and sensory-consent tensions → pair symbolic presence with accountable historical attribution and governance follow-through.
evidence_boundary: Strong for creator credits, format, date, host setting and conference remit; weak for participant interpretation and institutional consequence. Sources: [Yuning Chen project page](https://alienyuning.net/projects) and [Science History Institute conference record](https://www.sciencehistory.org/visit/events/gordon-cain-conference-2025/).

title: Morality Calculus / Food Theatre / Chewing It Over
creators: Yuning Chen with Elise Cachat, Adam Frank, Larissa Pschetz and collaborators
entity: Human–microbe hybrid fictions, fermentation microbes and shadow organisms
medium: Bioart installation; seven-session public dining theatre
occasions: Summerhall/Edinburgh Science Festival 2024; CHI 2026
publics: Free exhibition visitors, 47 dining participants, facilitators/researchers; microbes and donor organisms represented
summary:
This connected 2024–2026 project trajectory is led by Yuning Chen. *Morality Calculus* was developed with Elise Cachat and other scientific/artistic collaborators; its public Food Theatre informed the 2026 CHI paper *Chewing It Over* by Yuning Chen, Adam Frank and Larissa Pschetz. The installation and performance are treated as one case with two public phases rather than inflated into separate portfolio items.

The installation presents bread associated with a human–yeast cell hybrid experiment, fluorescent crumbs, cell-like blocks and evidence of organisms whose genes, enzymes or sera supported the work. The Food Theatre turns the question into an embodied public event: participants choose, discuss and eat vegetarian/vegan fermented foods given fictional human–microbe hybrid histories involving compression, auxotrophy, sterilisation, heat shock, isolation or bioremediation. Scales, magnets and “moral allergens” make the desire to quantify worth visibly incoherent.
publics_text: *Morality Calculus* was shown free at Summerhall’s War Memorial Gallery as part of Edinburgh Science Festival 2024, presented with ASCUS Art & Science and institutional partners (**D**). Seven two-hour lunchtime dining sessions involved 47 participants across ages, ethnicities and professions (**D**). Written notes, audio and opt-in visual records supported the 2026 CHI analysis. Free exhibition visitors are encountered publics; the 47 diners, hosts and researchers are participating publics. Synthetic-biology institutions and ethics bodies are decision-capable. Actual fermented microbes were present in food, while the human–microbial hybrids and suffering histories served as fictional proxies.
rq1: Mechanistic parts language hides microbial labour and “shadow organisms.” Ready-made ethics based on consumer safety, cannibalism taboo, paid human consent or causal distance can close inquiry before nonhuman relations are considered.
rq2: Tactics include material provenance display, hybrid-bread provocation, public dining, ingestion, fictional organism biographies grounded in real stresses, scientific staging, moral weights, disgust, corporal compassion and facilitation that values hesitation over consensus.
rq3: Bodily analogy can reveal shared vulnerability but may appropriate histories of refugees, disability, labour exploitation, racial violence or other human suffering to give microbes emotional weight. Human consent can become a moral pass while microbial nonparticipation remains unaddressed. Consumer risk may recentre the diner. Affect, disgust or empathy cannot be treated as a linear measure of ethical improvement.
evaluation: A mature public RQ3 case because it keeps contradiction and moral hesitation visible rather than claiming consensus.
configuration: Hidden microbial labour and premature moral closure → provenance installation plus consequential dining theatre → free festival visitors and 47 participating diners → strong qualitative evidence of disagreement and hesitation → proxy, appropriation, consent and commensurability tensions → treat moral hesitation as political capacity, not a quantified attitude outcome.
evidence_boundary: Strong peer-reviewed public-method evidence: seven sessions and 47 participants. Group talk was difficult to capture, session procedures changed after the first two groups, magnet counts are not quantitative data, the hybrid foods were fictional and no behavioural follow-up or microbial outcome was measured. Sources: [Edinburgh Science Festival/ASCUS exhibition record](https://www.ascus.org.uk/whats-on/earthsoilfilth-exhibition-esf2024-da9ep), [CHI 2026 DOI](https://doi.org/10.1145/3772318.3791048), [`references/chen2026chewing.md`](../chen2026chewing.md) and [`research/.../mthd-0079...md`](../../research/more-than-human-design-review/knowledge/papers/mthd-0079-2026-chewing-it-over-revealing-tensions-and-new-directions-for-more-than-human-relational-ethics-through-.md).

title: Hand-Substrate Interface
creators: Jen Liu, Daragh Byrne, Laura Devendorf; photographs © Robert Zacharias
entity: Fungi and the soil or organic substrates that support fungal growth
medium: Wearable soil-moisture sensing glove; exposed fingertip contact; LED display
occasions: Repeated forest tests; mushroom-foray research with a local club; CHI 2018
publics: Designer-wearer, mushroom foragers and citizen-science/mycology publics; CHI/HCI audiences; fungi and substrates represented
summary:
*Hand-Substrate Interface* (HSI) is a materially realised wearable prototype developed by Jen Liu with Daragh Byrne and Laura Devendorf during 2016–2017 and published at CHI 2018 as one of three *Design for Collaborative Survival* tools. Robert Zacharias photographed Figures 1 and 4 in the original paper; accordingly, the requested visual credit is recorded as **photographs © Robert Zacharias**, distinct from design authorship.

HSI reworks a soil-moisture sensor into a close-fitting glove. Conductive leather fingertip caps replace the usual rigid probes, mesh preserves contact with the earth, and a radial LED on the back of the hand displays approximate moisture. The wearer must insert and align their fingers in soil, leaf debris or other organic substrate, bringing digital conductivity measurement together with pressure, texture, dampness and the awkward bodily labour of digging. The prototype therefore makes the act of measurement itself an embodied encounter rather than offering a detached fungal-data dashboard.
publics_text: Liu developed the tools after attending multiple mushroom forays with a local club of approximately 600 members during 2016–2017 and tested HSI in forested areas on multiple occasions (**D**). The paper documents situated designer testing, not a public deployment study: it does not establish that club members used HSI or that a general audience encountered the prototype. Its documented public circulation is primarily through the CHI 2018 Best Paper publication and subsequent scholarly/design references (**D**). The designer-wearer is the directly participating public; mushroom-foraging, citizen-science, mycology, HCI and design communities are contextual or mediated publics. Fungi are not instrumented or consulted directly; their supporting substrates are touched and measured.
rq1: Fungi are commonly noticed through intermittent fruiting bodies, while the moisture and material conditions of their growth remain below ordinary public attention. Mycological and citizen-science practices can cultivate this knowledge, but they depend on situated expertise and repeated field contact that do not travel easily through conventional screens or general environmental communication.
rq2: The work combines bodily insertion, touch, conductive sensing, approximate LED feedback, wearable proximity and repeated forest testing. Replacing a pointed metal probe with fingers intentionally adds friction: wiggling, digging, alignment and imperfect measurement direct attention to substrate as a shared condition of fungal life. Its bridge is therefore sensory and relational as well as informational.
rq3: HSI measures electrical conductivity associated with substrate moisture, not fungal presence, feeling or intention. The human hand and a designer-set calibration determine what becomes legible. The paper explicitly notes lower accuracy than a rigid sensor and reflects mainly on Liu's own experience, so an evocative prototype must not be inflated into evidence of general public understanding, citizen-science reliability, fungal agency or ecological benefit. Direct contact may cultivate care, but it can also disturb substrate; access also depends on mobility, willingness to touch soil and entry to forest or foraging settings.
evaluation: A strong embodied-noticing prototype that productively refuses frictionless sensing, but a weak public-reach or action-outcome case; use it to distinguish contact with habitat conditions from access to fungal experience.
configuration: Hidden fungal-supporting conditions and specialist field knowledge → fingertip soil contact plus approximate conductivity-to-LED translation → designer-wearer and mediated foraging/HCI publics → documented iterative prototype experience → human calibration, access, disturbance and false-fidelity tensions → frame habitat contact as an invitation to inquiry, not access to a fungal umwelt or proof of benefit.
evidence_boundary: Strong for authorship, iterative construction, operation, forest testing and the authors' own reflexive interpretation; weak for exhibition reach, use by people other than the designer, durable practice change or consequence for fungi. The primary paper explicitly distinguishes experiencing substrate “along with” fungi from sensing fungi themselves. Ikeya, Barati and Wensveen's 2025 review records the supplied source-local citation **[136]** and image credit **© Robert Zacharias**; the primary paper further specifies that Zacharias photographed Figures 1 and 4 and was not a designer. Sources: [author-hosted CHI 2018 paper](https://jenliujenliu.com/Files/Liu_Collaborative_Survival.pdf), [CHI DOI](https://doi.org/10.1145/3173574.3173614), [`references/liu2018collaborative.md`](../liu2018collaborative.md), [`references/ikeya2025aesthetics.md`](../ikeya2025aesthetics.md) and the verified local full text.
entity_short: fungi and the soil or organic substrates that support fungal growth
format: wearable soil-moisture sensing glove with exposed fingertip contact and LED display

csv.rq2: The glove replaces rigid moisture probes with conductive fingertips, requiring direct insertion into soil while combining approximate LED readings with touch, digging and repeated situated forays.
